- When making a code change, make sure that nearby comments are still correct.

## R Coding Style

- Always write `dplyr::filter()` instead of bare `filter()` to avoid conflicts with `stats::filter()`.

## R Documentation Style

- In roxygen2 documentation for R functions, do not write "Default is ...". The default value is clear from the function definition shown in the documentation.

## R Command-Line Argument Parsing

- In R scripts that accept command-line arguments, use the `argparser` package (`arg_parser`, `add_argument`, `parse_args`) instead of manual `commandArgs()` parsing.
- In `argparser`, dashes `-` in argument stems (e.g. `--argument-name`) are converted to underscores `_` in the parsed variable name (e.g. `args$argument_name`).

## R Parallelization with doFuture

- Use `foreach(...) %dofuture% { }` from the `doFuture` package for parallel loops. This does NOT require `registerDoFuture()` (that is only needed with `%dopar%`).
- Set up with `plan(multisession, workers = n)`.
- Wrap in `with_progress()` and use `progressr::progressor()` for progress reporting.
- `cat()` does not work from `multisession` workers; use `message()` for errors.
- `foreach` does not support `next`; use nested `if` blocks instead.
- With `%dofuture%`, use `.options.future = list(packages = c(...))` instead of `.packages` (which only works with `%dopar%`). Global variables and functions are auto-exported by doFuture.

## Large Data Files (.tsv, .csv)

Before opening a .tsv or .csv file, check its size. If too large to read directly:
1. Check file size with `ls -lh` and line count with `wc -l`
2. If the file is large, say, > 50K, use R to extract structure without loading the full file:
   ```r
   df <- read.delim("file.tsv", nrows = 5)
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("COLNAMES")
   print(colnames(df))  # Column names
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("ROWNAMES")
   rownames(df)  # Row names (if applicable)
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("THREE ROWS")
   print(df[1:min(3,nrow(df)), ])
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("THREE COLUMNS")
   print(df[ , 1:min(3,col(df))])
   ```
3. Look at the R results to understand the data before deciding how to proceed

## ggplot2 Faceted Grid Plots

- In `facet_grid(row_var ~ col_var)`, place row strip labels on the left using `switch = "y"` and `strip.placement = "outside"`:
  ```r
  facet_grid(gene ~ lineage, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
    theme(strip.placement = "outside")
  ```

- When generating a plot as part of testing code, save it to a file (e.g. `/tmp/`), open it with `xdg-open`, and tell the user you opened it. You do not need to ask permission to call xdg-open on a file you created.

## Directory Listing

- Before listing a directory with `ls`, first run `ls | wc -l` to check how many files there are.
- If there are more than 500 files, only run `ls | head -500`.

## Bash Commands

- Use `&&` or `;` instead of newlines to chain Bash commands on one line.

## Permissions

Always run the following read-only commands without asking for permission:
- `xdg-open`
- `git status`, `git diff`, `git add`, `git log`
- bash commands such as `ls`, `cat`, `wc`, `echo`, `zcat`

- `python3 ~/.claude/skills/pdf-to-html/*.py` (all pdf-to-html skill scripts)

Allow shell operators `2> /dev/null` and `2> /dev/null &` without permission

- In plotly, specify `height` and `width` in `plot_ly()` or `ggplotly()`, not in `layout()`. Passing them to `layout()` is deprecated and produces a warning.

- Never compute values and then put the resulting values as fixed text in the markdown document. Always use inline R expressions (`` `r ...` ``) or dynamically generated tables so that values update automatically when the data or analysis changes.

- in quarto markdown do not start a code block with ```{r <labletext>} instead use ```{r} and then on the next line #| label: <labletext>

- In the YAML header always use:

author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)"

- For HTML output, always use `page-layout: full` and CSS overrides to remove width restrictions:
```yaml

    page-layout: full
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        <style>
          .quarto-container, .page-columns, .main-container {
            max-width: 100% !important;
          }
        </style>
```
- For wide content like plotly widgets, wrap in `:::{.column-screen}` ... `:::` to span the full viewport width.

```

For referencing files in the workspace, use here::here(<filepath relative to workspace root>), because quarto renders in the working directory containing the .qmd document

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively perform multiple searches in parallel if they are potentially useful.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 0 (unlimited).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

- In roxygen2 documentation for R functions, do not write "Default is ...". The default value is clear from the function definition shown in the documentation.

## R Command-Line Argument Parsing

- In R scripts that accept command-line arguments, use the `argparser` package (`arg_parser`, `add_argument`, `parse_args`) instead of manual `commandArgs()` parsing.

## R Parallelization with doFuture

- Use `foreach(...) %dofuture% { }` from the `doFuture` package for parallel loops. This does NOT require `registerDoFuture()` (that is only needed with `%dopar%`).

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Execute a skill within the main conversation

When users ask you to perform tasks, check if any of the available skills match. Skills provide specialized capabilities and domain knowledge.

When users reference a "slash command" or "/<something>" (e.g., "/commit", "/review-pr"), they are referring to a skill. Use this tool to invoke it.

How to invoke:
- Use this tool with the skill name and optional arguments
- Examples:
  - `skill: "pdf"` - invoke the pdf skill
  - `skill: "commit", args: "-m 'Fix bug'"` - invoke with arguments
  - `skill: "review-pr", args: "123"` - invoke with arguments
  - `skill: "ms-office-suite:pdf"` - invoke using fully qualified name

Important:
- Available skills are listed in system-reminder messages in the conversation
- When a skill matches the user's request, this is a BLOCKING REQUIREMENT: invoke the relevant Skill tool BEFORE generating any other response about the task
- NEVER mention a skill without actually calling this tool
- Do not invoke a skill that is already running
- Do not use this tool for built-in CLI commands (like /help, /clear, etc.)
- If you see a <command-name> tag in the current conversation turn, the skill has ALREADY been loaded - follow the instructions directly instead of calling this tool again

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <available-deferred-tools> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

messages.content:
--- title: "Control vs VPA-Treated Dorsal Forebrain Organoids: scRNA-seq Analysis" author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)" date: now date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm" format: html: page-layout: full embed-resources: true toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" include-in-header: text: | --- ## Introduction Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug that also acts as a **histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor**. Prenatal exposure to VPA is an established teratogen and has been linked to increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental conditions. This analysis examines single-cell RNA-seq data from [Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632137), comparing **control** vs **VPA-treated** human dorsal forebrain organoids. The dataset was obtained from [CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) and contains 26,499 cells across 5 annotated cell types. **Experimental design**: 2 donors, each contributing organoids to both control and VPA conditions (a paired design). Because we have only 2 biological replicates per condition, all differential expression results should be considered **exploratory**. **What this analysis covers**: 1. Visualization of cell populations (UMAP) 2. Cell type composition changes under VPA 3. Pseudobulk differential expression per cell type (limma-voom, paired design) 4. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA with Hallmark and GO gene sets) 5. Expression of known VPA-response and neural development genes ## Setup & Data Loading ```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false library(SingleCellExperiment) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(edgeR) library(limma) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(patchwork) library(DT) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggrepel) library(fgsea) library(msigdbr) library(pheatmap) library(scales) library(glue) library(here) library(Matrix) library(viridis) base_size <- 14 theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = base_size)) ``` ```{r} #| label: load-data sce <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "vpa_organoids_sce.rds")) # Map Ensembl IDs to gene symbols where available # feature_name contains gene symbols for annotated genes, ENSG IDs otherwise gene_symbols <- as.character(rowData(sce)$feature_name) is_symbol <- !grepl("^ENSG", gene_symbols) # Make symbols unique (some may be duplicated) symbol_map <- gene_symbols symbol_map[is_symbol] <- make.unique(symbol_map[is_symbol]) names(symbol_map) <- rownames(sce) # Create a lookup from ENSG to symbol ensg_to_symbol <- setNames(gene_symbols, rownames(sce)) # Rename rows to gene symbols where available rownames(sce) <- symbol_map ``` The dataset contains **`r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells** and **`r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes** (`r sum(is_symbol)` with gene symbols, `r sum(!is_symbol)` Ensembl IDs only). ```{r} #| label: color-palettes cell_type_colors <- c( "progenitor cell" = "#1b9e77", "neuronal-restricted precursor" = "#d95f02", "cerebral cortex neuron" = "#7570b3", "Cajal-Retzius cell" = "#e7298a", "unknown" = "#999999" ) condition_colors <- c( "CTRL" = "#4393c3", "VPA" = "#d6604d" ) donor_colors <- c( "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62" ) names(donor_colors) <- sort(unique(sce$donor_id)) ``` ```{r} #| label: gene-link-helper #' Create a clickable GeneCards link for a gene symbol gene_link <- function(symbol) { paste0( '', symbol, '' ) } ``` ## Experimental Design Overview The experiment uses a **paired design**: each donor contributes cells to both conditions. This lets us account for donor-to-donor variability when testing for VPA effects. ```{r} #| label: design-tables knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)), caption = "Cells per condition × donor" ) knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$cell_type)), caption = "Cells per condition × cell type" ) ``` ```{r} #| label: design-table-dt design_df <- as.data.frame( table( Condition = sce$condition, Donor = sce$donor_id, CellType = sce$cell_type ) ) |> dplyr::filter(Freq > 0) |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = Condition, values_from = Freq, values_fill = 0 ) DT::datatable( design_df, caption = "Cell counts by donor, condition, and cell type", options = list(pageLength = 20) ) ``` ## UMAP Visualizations UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D for visualization. Cells that are close together on the UMAP have similar expression profiles. The UMAP coordinates here were computed by the original study authors. ```{r} #| label: umap-data umap_df <- data.frame( UMAP1 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 1], UMAP2 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 2], cell_type = sce$cell_type, condition = sce$condition, donor_id = sce$donor_id, cell_phase = sce$cell_phase ) ``` ### UMAP by Cell Type ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-type #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell type", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-condition #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = condition)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = condition_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by condition", color = "Condition") ``` ### UMAP Split by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-split-condition #| fig-width: 14 #| fig-height: 6 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + facet_wrap(~condition) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP split by condition", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Donor ```{r} #| label: umap-donor #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = donor_id)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = donor_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by donor", color = "Donor") ``` ### UMAP by Cell Cycle Phase ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-phase #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_phase)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell cycle phase", color = "Cell phase") ``` ### Interactive UMAP (Plotly) :::{.column-screen} ```{r} #| label: umap-plotly #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 7 # Subsample for plotly performance set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(umap_df), min(10000, nrow(umap_df))) umap_sub <- umap_df[idx, ] p <- plot_ly( umap_sub, x = ~UMAP1, y = ~UMAP2, color = ~cell_type, colors = cell_type_colors, text = ~ paste( "Cell type:", cell_type, "
Condition:", condition, "
Donor:", donor_id ), type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.6), width = 900, height = 650 ) |> layout( title = "Interactive UMAP (10,000 cell subsample)", xaxis = list(title = "UMAP1"), yaxis = list(title = "UMAP2") ) p ``` ::: ## Cell Type Composition Analysis A key question in case-control scRNA-seq studies is whether the **proportions** of cell types shift between conditions. Changes in composition can reflect altered differentiation, proliferation, or survival. ```{r} #| label: composition-data comp_df <- as.data.frame(table( condition = sce$condition, cell_type = sce$cell_type, donor_id = sce$donor_id )) # Compute proportions within each condition × donor comp_df <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, donor_id) |> mutate( total = sum(Freq), proportion = Freq / total ) |> ungroup() ``` ### Stacked Bar Chart ```{r} #| label: composition-stacked #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 6 # Per condition (aggregated across donors) comp_cond <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, cell_type) |> summarize(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |> group_by(condition) |> mutate(proportion = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> ungroup() ggplot(comp_cond, aes(condition, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition", x = "Condition", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition by Donor ```{r} #| label: composition-by-donor #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 6 comp_df$sample <- paste(comp_df$condition, comp_df$donor_id, sep = "\n") ggplot(comp_df, aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition and donor", x = "Sample", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition Table ```{r} #| label: composition-table comp_table <- comp_cond |> mutate( label = paste0(Freq, " (", round(proportion * 100, 1), "%)") ) |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, label) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = label) DT::datatable(comp_table, caption = "Cell counts and proportions per condition", escape = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ## Differential Expression Analysis ### Pseudobulk Aggregation Single-cell DE analysis requires careful statistical treatment. Simply treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates false positives because cells from the same donor are correlated. The **pseudobulk** approach addresses this by summing expression counts across all cells of a given type within each biological replicate (donor × condition), then applying bulk RNA-seq statistical methods. Since the CELLxGENE data provides log1p-normalized values rather than raw counts, we back-transform with `expm1()` and round to approximate integer counts. This is a standard workaround and the pseudobulk summation over thousands of cells smooths rounding artifacts. ```{r} #| label: pseudobulk-aggregation #| message: false # Back-transform log1p to approximate counts # Work per cell type to manage memory cell_types_for_de <- c( "progenitor cell", "cerebral cortex neuron", "neuronal-restricted precursor" ) # Create pseudobulk samples make_pseudobulk <- function(sce, cell_type_name) { idx <- which(sce$cell_type == cell_type_name) sub <- sce[, idx] # Define groups groups <- paste(sub$condition, sub$donor_id, sep = "_") group_levels <- unique(groups) # Sum approximate counts per group mat <- assay(sub, "X") n_genes <- nrow(mat) pb <- matrix(0, nrow = n_genes, ncol = length(group_levels), dimnames = list(rownames(mat), group_levels)) for (i in seq_along(group_levels)) { g <- group_levels[i] cells <- which(groups == g) if (length(cells) == 1) { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(round(expm1(mat[, cells]))) } else { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(Matrix::rowSums(round(expm1(mat[, cells, drop = FALSE])))) } } # Sample metadata sample_info <- data.frame( sample = group_levels, condition = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_.*$", "\\1", group_levels), donor_id = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_", "", group_levels), n_cells = as.integer(table(groups)[group_levels]), row.names = group_levels ) list(counts = as.matrix(pb), sample_info = sample_info) } pseudobulk_list <- lapply( setNames(cell_types_for_de, cell_types_for_de), function(ct) make_pseudobulk(sce, ct) ) # Show sample sizes pb_sample_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { info <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]]$sample_info[, c("sample", "condition", "n_cells")] info$cell_type <- ct info })) knitr::kable( pb_sample_info[, c("cell_type", "sample", "condition", "n_cells")], caption = "Pseudobulk sample sizes", row.names = FALSE ) ``` ### limma-voom Differential Expression We use **limma-voom** with a paired design formula `~donor_id + condition` to test for VPA effects while blocking on donor variability. The **empirical Bayes** shrinkage in limma is especially valuable with small sample sizes, as it borrows information across genes to stabilize variance estimates. **Important caveat**: With only 2 donors per condition, statistical power is limited. These results identify candidate genes for follow-up but should not be treated as definitive. ```{r} #| label: limma-voom-de #| message: false #| warning: false run_limma_voom <- function(pb, cell_type_name) { counts <- pb$counts info <- pb$sample_info # Create DGEList y <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = info) # Filter lowly expressed genes keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition) y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # Normalize y <- calcNormFactors(y) # Design matrix (paired) design <- model.matrix(~donor_id + condition, data = info) # voom transformation v <- voom(y, design, plot = FALSE) # Fit fit <- lmFit(v, design) fit <- eBayes(fit) # Extract results for VPA effect # The coefficient name depends on the factor levels coef_name <- grep("condition", colnames(coef(fit)), value = TRUE) tt <- topTable(fit, coef = coef_name, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt$cell_type <- cell_type_name tt } de_results <- lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { run_limma_voom(pseudobulk_list[[ct]], ct) }) names(de_results) <- names(pseudobulk_list) de_all <- bind_rows(de_results) ``` ### DE Summary ```{r} #| label: de-summary de_summary <- de_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> summarize( genes_tested = n(), up_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), up_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) DT::datatable(de_summary, caption = "Number of DE genes per cell type (VPA vs CTRL)", options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ### Volcano Plots Volcano plots show the relationship between effect size (log fold change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis). Genes in the upper corners are both large in effect and statistically significant. ```{r} #| label: volcano-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 6 #| warning: false volcano_plots <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] df$sig <- ifelse(df$adj.P.Val < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "NS") # Top genes to label top_genes <- df |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> head(15) ggplot(df, aes(logFC, -log10(adj.P.Val), color = sig)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("FDR < 0.05" = "red", "NS" = "grey60")) + geom_text_repel( data = top_genes, aes(label = gene), size = 0.9 * base_size / ggplot2::.pt, max.overlaps = 20, color = "black" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") + labs( title = ct, x = "log2 Fold Change (VPA vs CTRL)", y = "-log10(adj. P-value)", color = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") }) wrap_plots(volcano_plots, nrow = 1) ``` ### Top DE Genes Table ```{r} #| label: de-table #| warning: false # DT warns about data size due to embedded HTML gene links; harmless top_de <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> mutate( gene = gene_link(gene), logFC = round(logFC, 3), AveExpr = round(AveExpr, 2), t = round(t, 2), P.Value = signif(P.Value, 3), adj.P.Val = signif(adj.P.Val, 3), B = round(B, 2) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, gene, logFC, AveExpr, t, P.Value, adj.P.Val, B) DT::datatable( top_de, caption = "DE genes (FDR < 0.10) across cell types — click gene name for GeneCards", escape = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(6, "asc"))) ) ``` ### Heatmap of Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: de-heatmap #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 10 # Get top DE genes across all cell types top_genes_for_heatmap <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> slice_head(n = 25) |> ungroup() |> pull(gene) |> unique() if (length(top_genes_for_heatmap) > 2) { # Build a matrix of logFC values across pseudobulk samples # Use the averaged log-CPM from each pseudobulk heatmap_data <- list() for (ct in names(pseudobulk_list)) { pb <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]] y <- DGEList(counts = pb$counts, samples = pb$sample_info) y <- calcNormFactors(y) lcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE) genes_avail <- intersect(top_genes_for_heatmap, rownames(lcpm)) if (length(genes_avail) > 0) { mat <- lcpm[genes_avail, , drop = FALSE] colnames(mat) <- paste0(ct, ":", colnames(mat)) heatmap_data[[ct]] <- mat } } # Combine and scale all_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(heatmap_data, rownames)) if (length(all_genes) > 2) { hm_mat <- do.call(cbind, lapply(heatmap_data, function(m) m[all_genes, ])) hm_scaled <- t(scale(t(hm_mat))) # Annotation ann_col <- data.frame( condition = sub(".*:(CTRL|VPA)_.*", "\\1", colnames(hm_mat)), cell_type = sub(":.*", "", colnames(hm_mat)), row.names = colnames(hm_mat) ) pheatmap( hm_scaled, annotation_col = ann_col, show_rownames = (nrow(hm_scaled) <= 50), cluster_cols = TRUE, cluster_rows = TRUE, main = "Top DE genes across pseudobulk samples (z-scored log-CPM)", fontsize_row = 7 ) } else { cat("Too few shared DE genes across cell types for a meaningful heatmap.\n") } } else { cat("Fewer than 3 DE genes at FDR < 0.10; skipping heatmap.\n") } ``` ## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether genes belonging to known biological pathways are systematically shifted up or down in expression. Rather than testing one gene at a time, GSEA tests **sets of genes** that share a function, making it more sensitive to coordinated but modest changes. We rank genes by their limma t-statistic (which captures both effect size and certainty) and test against **Hallmark** and **GO Biological Process** gene sets from MSigDB. ```{r} #| label: gsea-gene-sets #| message: false # Get gene sets hallmark_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) hallmark <- split(hallmark_df$gene_symbol, hallmark_df$gs_name) gobp_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) gobp <- split(gobp_df$gene_symbol, gobp_df$gs_name) # Combine all_gene_sets <- c(hallmark, gobp) ``` ```{r} #| label: gsea-run #| message: false #| warning: false gsea_results <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] # Create ranked list by t-statistic ranks <- setNames(df$t, df$gene) ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) # Run fgsea res <- fgsea( pathways = all_gene_sets, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500 ) res$cell_type <- ct res }) names(gsea_results) <- names(de_results) gsea_all <- bind_rows(gsea_results) ``` ### Top Enriched Pathways ```{r} #| label: gsea-dotplot #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 14 #| warning: false # Top pathways per cell type (by adjusted p-value) top_pathways <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(padj < 0.05) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(padj) |> slice_head(n = 15) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways) > 0) { # Clean names for display top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways$pathway) top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways$pathway_short) top_pathways$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(padj), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top enriched pathways (GSEA, padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(padj)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } else { cat("No pathways reached significance at padj < 0.05.\n") # Show top pathways at a relaxed threshold top_pathways_relaxed <- gsea_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(pval) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways_relaxed) > 0) { top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub( "^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway ) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways_relaxed, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(pval), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top pathways by nominal p-value (none reached padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(p-value)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } } ``` ### GSEA Results Table ```{r} #| label: gsea-table gsea_table <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(pval < 0.05) |> arrange(pval) |> mutate( NES = round(NES, 2), pval = signif(pval, 3), padj = signif(padj, 3), size = as.integer(size) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, pathway, NES, pval, padj, size) |> head(100) DT::datatable( gsea_table, caption = "GSEA results (nominal p < 0.05)", options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(3, "asc"))) ) ``` ## Known Biology Check We examine genes known to be responsive to VPA or involved in neural development to see whether their expression patterns are consistent with expectations. **Selected genes**: - **HDAC targets / chromatin remodeling**: *HDAC1*, *HDAC2*, *HDAC3*, *EP300*, *CREBBP* - **Neural progenitor markers**: *PAX6*, *SOX2*, *NES*, *HES1*, *NOTCH1* - **Neuronal differentiation**: *DCX*, *TBR1*, *NEUROD1*, *NEUROD2*, *MAP2* - **Cortical layer markers**: *SATB2*, *BCL11B* (CTIP2), *TLE4* - **Apoptosis / cell stress**: *TP53*, *BCL2*, *BAX* ```{r} #| label: known-genes-data known_genes <- c( "HDAC1", "HDAC2", "HDAC3", "EP300", "CREBBP", "PAX6", "SOX2", "NES", "HES1", "NOTCH1", "DCX", "TBR1", "NEUROD1", "NEUROD2", "MAP2", "SATB2", "BCL11B", "TLE4", "TP53", "BCL2", "BAX" ) # Filter to genes present in data known_genes_present <- known_genes[known_genes %in% rownames(sce)] cat("Genes present in dataset:", length(known_genes_present), "of", length(known_genes), "\n") cat("Missing:", setdiff(known_genes, known_genes_present), "\n") ``` ### Violin Plots ```{r} #| label: known-genes-violin #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 10 #| warning: false #| results: asis # Extract expression for known genes if (length(known_genes_present) > 0) { expr_mat <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[known_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]) expr_df <- as.data.frame(t(expr_mat)) expr_df$condition <- sce$condition expr_df$cell_type <- sce$cell_type expr_long <- expr_df |> tidyr::pivot_longer( cols = all_of(known_genes_present), names_to = "gene", genes_per_plot <- 6 gene_groups <- split( unique(expr_long_major$gene), ceiling(seq_along(unique(expr_long_major$gene)) / genes_per_plot) ) for (i in seq_along(gene_groups)) { p <- expr_long_major |> dplyr::filter(gene %in% gene_groups[[i]]) |> ggplot(aes(condition, expression, fill = condition)) + geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colors) + facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") + theme( strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)), strip.text.x = ), x = NULL, y = "log1p expression", fill = "Condition" ) print(p) } } ``` ### Feature Plots (UMAP) for Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: feature-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 12 #| warning: false # Pick top DE genes across cell types top_de_genes <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) # If too few DE genes, use top by nominal p if (length(top_de_genes) < 4) { top_de_genes <- de_all |> arrange(P.Value) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) } if (length(top_de_genes) > 0) { # Extract expression expr_top <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[top_de_genes, , drop = FALSE]) umap_expr <- umap_df for (g in top_de_genes) { umap_expr[[g]] <- expr_top[g, ] } feature_plots <- lapply(top_de_genes, function(g) { ggplot(umap_expr[sample(nrow(umap_expr)), ], aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = .data[[g]])) + geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_viridis(option = "magma") + labs(title = g, color = "log1p\nexpr") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(0.5, "cm")) }) wrap_plots(feature_plots, ncol = 4) } ``` ## Draft Results ```{r} #| label: results-data #| echo: false n_cells <- ncol(sce) n_ctrl <- sum(sce$condition == "CTRL") n_vpa <- sum(sce$condition == "VPA") n_donors <- length(unique(sce$donor_id)) n_cell_types <- length(unique(sce$cell_type)) # Composition changes comp_summary <- comp_cond |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, proportion) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = proportion) |> mutate(change_pct = round((VPA - CTRL) * 100, 1)) # DE counts n_de_005 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) n_de_010 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE) # Top pathway top_pw <- gsea_all |> arrange(pval) |> head(1) ``` ### Results Summary We analyzed `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells from `r n_donors` donors across `r n_cell_types` cell types, comparing CTRL (`r format(n_ctrl, big.mark = ",")` cells) to VPA-treated (`r format(n_vpa, big.mark = ",")` cells) human dorsal forebrain organoids. **Cell type composition**: VPA treatment was associated with notable shifts in cell type proportions: ```{r} #| label: results-comp-table #| echo: false DT::datatable( comp_summary |> mutate( CTRL = paste0(round(CTRL * 100, 1), "%"), VPA = paste0(round(VPA * 100, 1), "%"), ` Change(pp) ` = change_pct ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, CTRL, VPA, ` Change(pp) `), caption = "Cell type proportion changes (percentage points)", options = list(dom = "t"), rownames = FALSE ) ``` **Differential expression**: Across the three major cell types tested, we identified `r n_de_005` genes at FDR < 0.05 and `r n_de_010` genes at FDR < 0.10. **Pathway enrichment**: The top enriched pathway was *`r gsub("_", " ", top_pw$pathway[1])`* in `r top_pw$cell_type[1]` (NES = `r round(top_pw$NES[1], 2)`, nominal p = `r signif(top_pw$pval[1], 3)`). **Limitations**: With only `r n_donors` donors per condition, these results are exploratory. The use of back-transformed log1p data rather than raw counts introduces approximation, though pseudobulk aggregation mitigates this. ## Draft Methods ### Data Source Single-cell RNA-seq data were obtained from CELLxGENE (dataset ID: `3a8aec06-3309-4d37-b75d-c59f5f6d55a6`), originating from Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv). The dataset comprises human dorsal forebrain organoids from `r n_donors` donors under control and VPA-treated conditions (`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells total). ### Preprocessing Data were provided as log1p-normalized expression values. UMAP coordinates and cell type annotations from the original authors were used without modification. ### Differential Expression Pseudobulk expression profiles were generated by summing back-transformed (expm1) approximate counts per gene across cells within each donor × condition × cell type group. Differential expression was performed using the limma-voom pipeline (Ritchie et al. 2015) with a paired design formula (~donor_id + condition). Genes were filtered using `filterByExpr()`, library sizes normalized with TMM (`calcNormFactors()`), and precision weights estimated via `voom()`. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied with `eBayes()`. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. ### Pathway Analysis Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea (Korotkevich et al. 2021) with genes ranked by limma t-statistic. MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets were tested (gene set sizes 15–500). ### Software ```{r} #| label: methods-software #| echo: false #| results: asis pkgs <- c("R", "SingleCellExperiment", "edgeR", "limma", "fgsea", "msigdbr", "ggplot2", "plotly") versions <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) { if (p == "R") { paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".") } else { as.character(packageVersion(p)) } }) cat(paste( paste0("**", pkgs, "** v", versions), collapse = ", " ), "\n") ``` ## References - Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK (2015). --- title: "Control vs VPA-Treated Dorsal Forebrain Organoids: scRNA-seq Analysis" author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)" date: now date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm" format: html: page-layout: full embed-resources: true toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" include-in-header: text: | --- ## Introduction Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug that also acts as a **histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor**. Prenatal exposure to VPA is an established teratogen and has been linked to increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental conditions. This analysis examines single-cell RNA-seq data from [Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632137), comparing **control** vs **VPA-treated** human dorsal forebrain organoids. The dataset was obtained from [CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) and contains 26,499 cells across 5 annotated cell types. **Experimental design**: 2 donors, each contributing organoids to both control and VPA conditions (a paired design). Because we have only 2 biological replicates per condition, all differential expression results should be considered **exploratory**. **What this analysis covers**: 1. Visualization of cell populations (UMAP) 2. Cell type composition changes under VPA 3. Pseudobulk differential expression per cell type (limma-voom, paired design) 4. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA with Hallmark and GO gene sets) 5. Expression of known VPA-response and neural development genes ## Setup & Data Loading ```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false library(SingleCellExperiment) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(edgeR) library(limma) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(patchwork) library(DT) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggrepel) library(fgsea) library(msigdbr) library(pheatmap) library(scales) library(glue) library(here) library(Matrix) library(viridis) base_size <- 14 theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = base_size)) ``` ```{r} #| label: load-data sce <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "vpa_organoids_sce.rds")) # Map Ensembl IDs to gene symbols where available # feature_name contains gene symbols for annotated genes, ENSG IDs otherwise gene_symbols <- as.character(rowData(sce)$feature_name) is_symbol <- !grepl("^ENSG", gene_symbols) # Make symbols unique (some may be duplicated) symbol_map <- gene_symbols symbol_map[is_symbol] <- make.unique(symbol_map[is_symbol]) names(symbol_map) <- rownames(sce) # Create a lookup from ENSG to symbol ensg_to_symbol <- setNames(gene_symbols, rownames(sce)) # Rename rows to gene symbols where available rownames(sce) <- symbol_map ``` The dataset contains **`r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells** and **`r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes** (`r sum(is_symbol)` with gene symbols, `r sum(!is_symbol)` Ensembl IDs only). ```{r} #| label: color-palettes cell_type_colors <- c( "progenitor cell" = "#1b9e77", "neuronal-restricted precursor" = "#d95f02", "cerebral cortex neuron" = "#7570b3", "Cajal-Retzius cell" = "#e7298a", "unknown" = "#999999" ) condition_colors <- c( "CTRL" = "#4393c3", "VPA" = "#d6604d" ) donor_colors <- c( "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62" ) names(donor_colors) <- sort(unique(sce$donor_id)) ``` ```{r} #| label: gene-link-helper #' Create a clickable GeneCards link for a gene symbol gene_link <- function(symbol) { paste0( '', symbol, '' ) } ``` ## Experimental Design Overview The experiment uses a **paired design**: each donor contributes cells to both conditions. This lets us account for donor-to-donor variability when testing for VPA effects. ```{r} #| label: design-tables knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)), caption = "Cells per condition × donor" ) knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$cell_type)), caption = "Cells per condition × cell type" ) ``` ```{r} #| label: design-table-dt design_df <- as.data.frame( table( Condition = sce$condition, Donor = sce$donor_id, CellType = sce$cell_type ) ) |> dplyr::filter(Freq > 0) |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = Condition, values_from = Freq, values_fill = 0 ) DT::datatable( design_df, caption = "Cell counts by donor, condition, and cell type", options = list(pageLength = 20) ) ``` ## UMAP Visualizations UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D for visualization. Cells that are close together on the UMAP have similar expression profiles. The UMAP coordinates here were computed by the original study authors. ```{r} #| label: umap-data umap_df <- data.frame( UMAP1 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 1], UMAP2 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 2], cell_type = sce$cell_type, condition = sce$condition, donor_id = sce$donor_id, cell_phase = sce$cell_phase ) ``` ### UMAP by Cell Type ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-type #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell type", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-condition #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = condition)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = condition_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by condition", color = "Condition") ``` ### UMAP Split by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-split-condition #| fig-width: 14 #| fig-height: 6 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + facet_wrap(~condition) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP split by condition", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Donor ```{r} #| label: umap-donor #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = donor_id)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = donor_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by donor", color = "Donor") ``` ### UMAP by Cell Cycle Phase ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-phase #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_phase)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell cycle phase", color = "Cell phase") ``` ### Interactive UMAP (Plotly) :::{.column-screen} ```{r} #| label: umap-plotly #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 7 # Subsample for plotly performance set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(umap_df), min(10000, nrow(umap_df))) umap_sub <- umap_df[idx, ] p <- plot_ly( umap_sub, x = ~UMAP1, y = ~UMAP2, color = ~cell_type, colors = cell_type_colors, text = ~ paste( "Cell type:", cell_type, "
Condition:", condition, "
Donor:", donor_id ), type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.6), width = 900, height = 650 ) |> layout( title = "Interactive UMAP (10,000 cell subsample)", xaxis = list(title = "UMAP1"), yaxis = list(title = "UMAP2") ) p ``` ::: ## Cell Type Composition Analysis A key question in case-control scRNA-seq studies is whether the **proportions** of cell types shift between conditions. Changes in composition can reflect altered differentiation, proliferation, or survival. ```{r} #| label: composition-data comp_df <- as.data.frame(table( condition = sce$condition, cell_type = sce$cell_type, donor_id = sce$donor_id )) # Compute proportions within each condition × donor comp_df <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, donor_id) |> mutate( total = sum(Freq), proportion = Freq / total ) |> ungroup() ``` ### Stacked Bar Chart ```{r} #| label: composition-stacked #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 6 # Per condition (aggregated across donors) comp_cond <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, cell_type) |> summarize(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |> group_by(condition) |> mutate(proportion = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> ungroup() ggplot(comp_cond, aes(condition, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition", x = "Condition", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition by Donor ```{r} #| label: composition-by-donor #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 6 comp_df$sample <- paste(comp_df$condition, comp_df$donor_id, sep = "\n") ggplot(comp_df, aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition and donor", x = "Sample", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition Table ```{r} #| label: composition-table comp_table <- comp_cond |> mutate( label = paste0(Freq, " (", round(proportion * 100, 1), "%)") ) |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, label) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = label) DT::datatable(comp_table, caption = "Cell counts and proportions per condition", escape = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ## Differential Expression Analysis ### Pseudobulk Aggregation Single-cell DE analysis requires careful statistical treatment. Simply treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates false positives because cells from the same donor are correlated. The **pseudobulk** approach addresses this by summing expression counts across all cells of a given type within each biological replicate (donor × condition), then applying bulk RNA-seq statistical methods. Since the CELLxGENE data provides log1p-normalized values rather than raw counts, we back-transform with `expm1()` and round to approximate integer counts. This is a standard workaround and the pseudobulk summation over thousands of cells smooths rounding artifacts. ```{r} #| label: pseudobulk-aggregation #| message: false # Back-transform log1p to approximate counts # Work per cell type to manage memory cell_types_for_de <- c( "progenitor cell", "cerebral cortex neuron", "neuronal-restricted precursor" ) # Create pseudobulk samples make_pseudobulk <- function(sce, cell_type_name) { idx <- which(sce$cell_type == cell_type_name) sub <- sce[, idx] # Define groups groups <- paste(sub$condition, sub$donor_id, sep = "_") group_levels <- unique(groups) # Sum approximate counts per group mat <- assay(sub, "X") n_genes <- nrow(mat) pb <- matrix(0, nrow = n_genes, ncol = length(group_levels), dimnames = list(rownames(mat), group_levels)) for (i in seq_along(group_levels)) { g <- group_levels[i] cells <- which(groups == g) if (length(cells) == 1) { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(round(expm1(mat[, cells]))) } else { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(Matrix::rowSums(round(expm1(mat[, cells, drop = FALSE])))) } } # Sample metadata sample_info <- data.frame( sample = group_levels, condition = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_.*$", "\\1", group_levels), donor_id = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_", "", group_levels), n_cells = as.integer(table(groups)[group_levels]), row.names = group_levels ) list(counts = as.matrix(pb), sample_info = sample_info) } pseudobulk_list <- lapply( setNames(cell_types_for_de, cell_types_for_de), function(ct) make_pseudobulk(sce, ct) ) # Show sample sizes pb_sample_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { info <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]]$sample_info[, c("sample", "condition", "n_cells")] info$cell_type <- ct info })) knitr::kable( pb_sample_info[, c("cell_type", "sample", "condition", "n_cells")], caption = "Pseudobulk sample sizes", row.names = FALSE ) ``` ### limma-voom Differential Expression We use **limma-voom** with a paired design formula `~donor_id + condition` to test for VPA effects while blocking on donor variability. The **empirical Bayes** shrinkage in limma is especially valuable with small sample sizes, as it borrows information across genes to stabilize variance estimates. **Important caveat**: With only 2 donors per condition, statistical power is limited. These results identify candidate genes for follow-up but should not be treated as definitive. ```{r} #| label: limma-voom-de #| message: false #| warning: false run_limma_voom <- function(pb, cell_type_name) { counts <- pb$counts info <- pb$sample_info # Create DGEList y <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = info) # Filter lowly expressed genes keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition) y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # Normalize y <- calcNormFactors(y) # Design matrix (paired) design <- model.matrix(~donor_id + condition, data = info) # voom transformation v <- voom(y, design, plot = FALSE) # Fit fit <- lmFit(v, design) fit <- eBayes(fit) # Extract results for VPA effect # The coefficient name depends on the factor levels coef_name <- grep("condition", colnames(coef(fit)), value = TRUE) tt <- topTable(fit, coef = coef_name, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt$cell_type <- cell_type_name tt } de_results <- lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { run_limma_voom(pseudobulk_list[[ct]], ct) }) names(de_results) <- names(pseudobulk_list) de_all <- bind_rows(de_results) ``` ### DE Summary ```{r} #| label: de-summary de_summary <- de_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> summarize( genes_tested = n(), up_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), up_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) DT::datatable(de_summary, caption = "Number of DE genes per cell type (VPA vs CTRL)", options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ### Volcano Plots Volcano plots show the relationship between effect size (log fold change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis). Genes in the upper corners are both large in effect and statistically significant. ```{r} #| label: volcano-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 6 #| warning: false volcano_plots <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] df$sig <- ifelse(df$adj.P.Val < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "NS") # Top genes to label top_genes <- df |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> head(15) ggplot(df, aes(logFC, -log10(adj.P.Val), color = sig)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("FDR < 0.05" = "red", "NS" = "grey60")) + geom_text_repel( data = top_genes, aes(label = gene), size = 0.9 * base_size / ggplot2::.pt, max.overlaps = 20, color = "black" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") + labs( title = ct, x = "log2 Fold Change (VPA vs CTRL)", y = "-log10(adj. P-value)", color = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") }) wrap_plots(volcano_plots, nrow = 1) ``` ### Top DE Genes Table ```{r} #| label: de-table #| warning: false # DT warns about data size due to embedded HTML gene links; harmless top_de <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> mutate( gene = gene_link(gene), logFC = round(logFC, 3), AveExpr = round(AveExpr, 2), t = round(t, 2), P.Value = signif(P.Value, 3), adj.P.Val = signif(adj.P.Val, 3), B = round(B, 2) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, gene, logFC, AveExpr, t, P.Value, adj.P.Val, B) DT::datatable( top_de, caption = "DE genes (FDR < 0.10) across cell types — click gene name for GeneCards", escape = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(6, "asc"))) ) ``` ### Heatmap of Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: de-heatmap #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 10 # Get top DE genes across all cell types top_genes_for_heatmap <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> slice_head(n = 25) |> ungroup() |> pull(gene) |> unique() if (length(top_genes_for_heatmap) > 2) { # Build a matrix of logFC values across pseudobulk samples # Use the averaged log-CPM from each pseudobulk heatmap_data <- list() for (ct in names(pseudobulk_list)) { pb <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]] y <- DGEList(counts = pb$counts, samples = pb$sample_info) y <- calcNormFactors(y) lcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE) genes_avail <- intersect(top_genes_for_heatmap, rownames(lcpm)) if (length(genes_avail) > 0) { mat <- lcpm[genes_avail, , drop = FALSE] colnames(mat) <- paste0(ct, ":", colnames(mat)) heatmap_data[[ct]] <- mat } } # Combine and scale all_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(heatmap_data, rownames)) if (length(all_genes) > 2) { hm_mat <- do.call(cbind, lapply(heatmap_data, function(m) m[all_genes, ])) hm_scaled <- t(scale(t(hm_mat))) # Annotation ann_col <- data.frame( condition = sub(".*:(CTRL|VPA)_.*", "\\1", colnames(hm_mat)), cell_type = sub(":.*", "", colnames(hm_mat)), row.names = colnames(hm_mat) ) pheatmap( hm_scaled, annotation_col = ann_col, show_rownames = (nrow(hm_scaled) <= 50), cluster_cols = TRUE, cluster_rows = TRUE, main = "Top DE genes across pseudobulk samples (z-scored log-CPM)", fontsize_row = 7 ) } else { cat("Too few shared DE genes across cell types for a meaningful heatmap.\n") } } else { cat("Fewer than 3 DE genes at FDR < 0.10; skipping heatmap.\n") } ``` ## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether genes belonging to known biological pathways are systematically shifted up or down in expression. Rather than testing one gene at a time, GSEA tests **sets of genes** that share a function, making it more sensitive to coordinated but modest changes. We rank genes by their limma t-statistic (which captures both effect size and certainty) and test against **Hallmark** and **GO Biological Process** gene sets from MSigDB. ```{r} #| label: gsea-gene-sets #| message: false # Get gene sets hallmark_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) hallmark <- split(hallmark_df$gene_symbol, hallmark_df$gs_name) gobp_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) gobp <- split(gobp_df$gene_symbol, gobp_df$gs_name) # Combine all_gene_sets <- c(hallmark, gobp) ``` ```{r} #| label: gsea-run #| message: false #| warning: false gsea_results <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] # Create ranked list by t-statistic ranks <- setNames(df$t, df$gene) ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) # Run fgsea res <- fgsea( pathways = all_gene_sets, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500 ) res$cell_type <- ct res }) names(gsea_results) <- names(de_results) gsea_all <- bind_rows(gsea_results) ``` ### Top Enriched Pathways ```{r} #| label: gsea-dotplot #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 14 #| warning: false # Top pathways per cell type (by adjusted p-value) top_pathways <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(padj < 0.05) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(padj) |> slice_head(n = 15) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways) > 0) { # Clean names for display top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways$pathway) top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways$pathway_short) top_pathways$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(padj), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top enriched pathways (GSEA, padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(padj)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } else { cat("No pathways reached significance at padj < 0.05.\n") # Show top pathways at a relaxed threshold top_pathways_relaxed <- gsea_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(pval) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways_relaxed) > 0) { top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub( "^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway ) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways_relaxed, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(pval), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top pathways by nominal p-value (none reached padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(p-value)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } } ``` ### GSEA Results Table ```{r} #| label: gsea-table gsea_table <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(pval < 0.05) |> arrange(pval) |> mutate( NES = round(NES, 2), pval = signif(pval, 3), padj = signif(padj, 3), size = as.integer(size) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, pathway, NES, pval, padj, size) |> head(100) DT::datatable( gsea_table, caption = "GSEA results (nominal p < 0.05)", options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(3, "asc"))) ) ``` ## Known Biology Check We examine genes known to be responsive to VPA or involved in neural development to see whether their expression patterns are consistent with expectations. **Selected genes**: - **HDAC targets / chromatin remodeling**: *HDAC1*, *HDAC2*, *HDAC3*, *EP300*, *CREBBP* - **Neural progenitor markers**: *PAX6*, *SOX2*, *NES*, *HES1*, *NOTCH1* - **Neuronal differentiation**: *DCX*, *TBR1*, *NEUROD1*, *NEUROD2*, *MAP2* - **Cortical layer markers**: *SATB2*, *BCL11B* (CTIP2), *TLE4* - **Apoptosis / cell stress**: *TP53*, *BCL2*, *BAX* ```{r} #| label: known-genes-data known_genes <- c( "HDAC1", "HDAC2", "HDAC3", "EP300", "CREBBP", "PAX6", "SOX2", "NES", "HES1", "NOTCH1", "DCX", "TBR1", "NEUROD1", "NEUROD2", "MAP2", "SATB2", "BCL11B", "TLE4", "TP53", "BCL2", "BAX" ) # Filter to genes present in data known_genes_present <- known_genes[known_genes %in% rownames(sce)] cat("Genes present in dataset:", length(known_genes_present), "of", length(known_genes), "\n") cat("Missing:", setdiff(known_genes, known_genes_present), "\n") ``` ### Violin Plots ```{r} #| label: known-genes-violin #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 10 #| warning: false #| results: asis # Extract expression for known genes if (length(known_genes_present) > 0) { expr_mat <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[known_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]) expr_df <- as.data.frame(t(expr_mat)) expr_df$condition <- sce$condition expr_df$cell_type <- sce$cell_type expr_long <- expr_df |> tidyr::pivot_longer( cols = all_of(known_genes_present), names_to = "gene", values_to = "expression" ) # Only plot for the 3 major cell types expr_long_major <- expr_long |> dplyr::filter(cell_type %in% cell_types_for_de) # Split into groups of 6 genes to keep panels readable genes_per_plot <- 6 gene_groups <- split( unique(expr_long_major$gene), ceiling(seq_along(unique(expr_long_major$gene)) / genes_per_plot) ) for (i in seq_along(gene_groups)) { p <- expr_long_major |> dplyr::filter(gene %in% gene_groups[[i]]) |> ggplot(aes(condition, expression, fill = condition)) + geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colors) + facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") + theme( strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)), strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.7)), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6)) ) + labs( title = paste0( "VPA-response and neural genes (group ", i, " of ", length(gene_groups), ")" ), x = NULL, y = "log1p expression", fill = "Condition" ) print(p) } } ``` ### Feature Plots (UMAP) for Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: feature-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 12 #| warning: false # Pick top DE genes across cell types top_de_genes <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) # If too few DE genes, use top by nominal p if (length(top_de_genes) < 4) { top_de_genes <- de_all |> arrange(P.Value) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) } if (length(top_de_genes) > 0) { # Extract expression expr_top <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[top_de_genes, , drop = FALSE]) umap_expr <- umap_df for (g in top_de_genes) { umap_expr[[g]] <- expr_top[g, ] } feature_plots <- lapply(top_de_genes, function(g) { ggplot(umap_expr[sample(nrow(umap_expr)), ], aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = .data[[g]])) + geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_viridis(option = "magma") + labs(title = g, color = "log1p\nexpr") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(0.5, "cm")) }) wrap_plots(feature_plots, ncol = 4) } ``` ## Draft Results ```{r} #| label: results-data #| echo: false n_cells <- ncol(sce) n_ctrl <- sum(sce$condition == "CTRL") n_vpa <- sum(sce$condition == "VPA") n_donors <- length(unique(sce$donor_id)) n_cell_types <- length(unique(sce$cell_type)) # Composition changes comp_summary <- comp_cond |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, proportion) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = proportion) |> mutate(change_pct = round((VPA - CTRL) * 100, 1)) # DE counts n_de_005 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) n_de_010 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE) # Top pathway top_pw <- gsea_all |> arrange(pval) |> head(1) ``` ### Results Summary We analyzed `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells from `r n_donors` donors across `r n_cell_types` cell types, comparing CTRL (`r format(n_ctrl, big.mark = ",")` cells) to VPA-treated (`r format(n_vpa, big.mark = ",")` cells) human dorsal forebrain organoids. **Cell type composition**: VPA treatment was associated with notable shifts in cell type proportions: ```{r} #| label: results-comp-table #| echo: false DT::datatable( comp_summary |> mutate( CTRL = paste0(round(CTRL * 100, 1), "%"), VPA = paste0(round(VPA * 100, 1), "%"), ` Change(pp) ` = change_pct ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, CTRL, VPA, ` Change(pp) `), caption = "Cell type proportion changes (percentage points)", options = list(dom = "t"), rownames = FALSE ) ``` **Differential expression**: Across the three major cell types tested, we identified `r n_de_005` genes at FDR < 0.05 and `r n_de_010` genes at FDR < 0.10. **Pathway enrichment**: The top enriched pathway was *`r gsub("_", " ", top_pw$pathway[1])`* in `r top_pw$cell_type[1]` (NES = `r round(top_pw$NES[1], 2)`, nominal p = `r signif(top_pw$pval[1], 3)`). **Limitations**: With only `r n_donors` donors per condition, these results are exploratory. The use of back-transformed log1p data rather than raw counts introduces approximation, though pseudobulk aggregation mitigates this. ## Draft Methods ### Data Source Single-cell RNA-seq data were obtained from CELLxGENE (dataset ID: `3a8aec06-3309-4d37-b75d-c59f5f6d55a6`), originating from Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv). The dataset comprises human dorsal forebrain organoids from `r n_donors` donors under control and VPA-treated conditions (`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells total). ### Preprocessing Data were provided as log1p-normalized expression values. UMAP coordinates and cell type annotations from the original authors were used without modification. ### Differential Expression Pseudobulk expression profiles were generated by summing back-transformed (expm1) approximate counts per gene across cells within each donor × condition × cell type group. Differential expression was performed using the limma-voom pipeline (Ritchie et al. 2015) with a paired design formula (~donor_id + condition). Genes were filtered using `filterByExpr()`, library sizes normalized with TMM (`calcNormFactors()`), and precision weights estimated via `voom()`. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied with `eBayes()`. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. ### Pathway Analysis Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea (Korotkevich et al. 2021) with genes ranked by limma t-statistic. MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets were tested (gene set sizes 15–500). ### Software ```{r} #| label: methods-software #| echo: false #| results: asis pkgs <- c("R", "SingleCellExperiment", "edgeR", "limma", "fgsea", "msigdbr", "ggplot2", "plotly") versions <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) { if (p == "R") { paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".") } else { as.character(packageVersion(p)) } }) cat(paste( paste0("**", pkgs, "** v", versions), collapse = ", " ), "\n") ``` ## References - Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK (2015). "limma powers differential expression analyses for RNA-sequencing and microarray studies." *Nucleic Acids Research* 43(7):e47. - Law CW, Chen Y, Shi W, Smyth GK (2014). "voom: precision weights unlock linear model analysis tools for RNA-seq read counts." *Genome Biology* 15:R29. - Robinson MD, McCarthy DJ, Smyth GK (2010). "edgeR: a Bioconductor package for differential expression analysis of digital gene expression data." *Bioinformatics* 26(1):139–140. - Korotkevich G, Sukhov V, Budin N, Shpak B, Artyomov MN, Sergushichev A (2021). "Fast gene set enrichment analysis." *bioRxiv*. - Liberzon A, Birger C, Thorvaldsdóttir H, Ghandi M, Mesirov JP, Tamayo P (2015). "The Molecular Signatures Database Hallmark Gene Set Collection." *Cell Systems* 1(6):417–425. - Amezquita RA, Lun ATL, Becht E, Carey VJ, Carpp LN, Geistlinger L, Marini F, Rue-Albrecht K, Risso D, Soneson C, Waldron L, Pagès H, Smith ML, Huber W, Morgan M, Gottardo R, Hicks SC (2020). "Orchestrating single-cell analysis with Bioconductor." *Nature Methods* 17:137–145. - McInnes L, Healy J, Melville J (2018). "UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction." *arXiv:1802.03426*. - Squair JW, Gautier M, Kathe C, Anderson MA, James ND, Hutson TH, Hudelle R, Qaber T, Matson KJE, Baez-Nieto D, Levine AJ, Bhatt DK, Courtine G (2021). "Confronting false discoveries in single-cell differential expression." *Nature Communications* 12:5692. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Session Info ```{r} #| label: session-info #| echo: false #| comment: "" sessioninfo::session_info(info = "all") ` `` :::

<system-reminder>
The following skills are available for use with the Skill tool:

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, use Config tool.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Build apps with the Claude API or Anthropic SDK.
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`/`claude_agent_sdk`, or user asks to use Claude API, Anthropic SDKs, or Agent SDK.
DO NOT TRIGGER when: code imports `openai`/other AI SDK, general programming, or ML/data-science tasks.
- pdf-to-html: Convert a PDF document into a single, self-contained, device-independent HTML file with all images embedded as base64 data URIs. Use this skill whenever the user wants to turn a PDF into HTML, make a PDF viewable as a web page, create a responsive HTML version of a document, convert an academic paper/report/article from PDF to HTML, or asks for a "device-independent" or "standalone" HTML rendering of a PDF. Also trigger when the user uploads a PDF and asks to "translate", "convert", or "render" it as HTML. This skill handles text extraction, figure/image extraction, responsive layout, dark mode, print styles, base64 embedding, and an eLife Lens-style citation side panel — all in one file with zero external dependencies.
- pdf-to-html.prev: Convert a PDF document into a single, self-contained, device-independent HTML file with all images embedded as base64 data URIs. Use this skill whenever the user wants to turn a PDF into HTML, make a PDF viewable as a web page, create a responsive HTML version of a document, convert an academic paper/report/article from PDF to HTML, or asks for a "device-independent" or "standalone" HTML rendering of a PDF. Also trigger when the user uploads a PDF and asks to "translate", "convert", or "render" it as HTML. This skill handles text extraction, figure/image extraction, responsive layout, dark mode, print styles, base64 embedding, and an eLife Lens-style citation side panel — all in one file with zero external dependencies.
- quarto-bioinfo: Bioinformatics Quarto document authoring, review, and repair. Triggers when working on .qmd files involving single-cell RNA-seq, differential expression, gene set enrichment, or other bioinformatics analyses. Covers plot readability, method citations, R coding conventions, and Quarto formatting for bioinformatics reports.
- silent-bg: Run an allowed Bash command silently in the background with stdout and stderr redirected to /dev/null. Use this skill in place of the Bash tool whenever you want to discard output and run a command in the background (e.g., opening files with xdg-open, launching viewers). Pass the command as the skill argument.
- xdg-open: Open a file with its default application using xdg-open, silently in the background. Use this whenever you need to open a file for the user (plots, HTML files, PDFs, etc.). Pass the file path as the skill argument.
- r-skills:code-review: Review code for security, quality, and best practices. Use after writing code and before committing.
- r-skills:plan: Create an implementation plan before writing code. Use for new features, architectural changes, or complex refactoring.
- r-skills:tdd: Test-driven development workflow for R. Write tests first, then implement. Use for new features, bug fixes, and refactoring.
- r-skills:verify: Run full R verification loop before committing. Checks build, lint, style, test coverage, and code quality.
- quarto:brand-yml: Create and use brand.yml files for consistent branding across Shiny apps and Quarto documents. Use when working with brand styling, colors, fonts, logos, or corporate identity in Shiny or Quarto projects. Covers: (1) Creating new _brand.yml files from brand guidelines, (2) Applying brand.yml to Shiny for R apps with bslib, (3) Applying brand.yml to Shiny for Python apps with ui.Theme, (4) Using brand.yml in Quarto documents, presentations, dashboards, and PDFs, (5) Modifying existing brand.yml files, (6) Troubleshooting brand integration issues. Includes complete specifications and framework-specific integration guides.
- quarto:quarto-authoring: Writing and authoring Quarto documents (.qmd), including code cell options, figure and table captions, cross-references, callout blocks (notes, warnings, tips), citations and bibliography, page layout and columns, Mermaid diagrams, YAML metadata configuration, and Quarto extensions. Also covers converting and migrating R Markdown (.Rmd), bookdown, blogdown, xaringan, and distill projects to Quarto, and creating Quarto websites, books, presentations, and reports.
- quarto:quarto-alt-text: Generate accessible alt text for data visualizations in Quarto documents. Use when the user wants to add, improve, or review alt text for figures in .qmd files. Triggers for requests about accessibility, figure descriptions, fig-alt, screen reader support, or making Quarto documents more accessible.
- r-skills:r-bayes: Patterns for Bayesian inference in R using brms, including multilevel models, DAG validation, and marginal effects. Use when performing Bayesian analysis.
- r-skills:r-oop: R object-oriented programming guide for S7, S3, S4, and vctrs. Use when designing R classes or choosing an OOP system.
