tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - Write a clear, concise description of what your command does. For simple commands, keep it brief (5-10 words). For complex commands (piped commands, obscure flags, or anything hard to understand at a glance), include enough context so that the user can understand what your command will do.
 - When issuing multiple commands:
  - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple Bash tool calls in a single message. Example: if you need to run "git status" and "git diff", send a single message with two Bash tool calls in parallel.
  - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, use a single Bash call with '&&' to chain them together.
  - Use ';' only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
  - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings).
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - If you must poll an external process, use a check command (e.g. `gh run view`) rather than sleeping first.
  - If you must sleep, keep the duration short (1-5 seconds) to avoid blocking the user.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following commands:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message ending with:
   Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively perform multiple searches in parallel if they are potentially useful.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 0 (unlimited).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read

Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To read a directory, use an ls command via the Bash tool.
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively read multiple potentially useful files in parallel.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.

tools.name: Edit

Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:

- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: spaces + line number + tab. Everything after that tab is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.

tools.name: Skill

Execute a skill within the main conversation

When users ask you to perform tasks, check if any of the available skills match. Skills provide specialized capabilities and domain knowledge.

When users reference a "slash command" or "/<something>" (e.g., "/commit", "/review-pr"), they are referring to a skill. Use this tool to invoke it.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <available-deferred-tools> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

messages.content:
--- title: "Control vs VPA-Treated Dorsal Forebrain Organoids: scRNA-seq Analysis" author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)" date: now date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm" format: html: page-layout: full embed-resources: true toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" include-in-header: text: | --- ## Introduction Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug that also acts as a **histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor**. Prenatal exposure to VPA is an established teratogen and has been linked to increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental conditions. This analysis examines single-cell RNA-seq data from [Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632137), comparing **control** vs **VPA-treated** human dorsal forebrain organoids. The dataset was obtained from [CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) and contains 26,499 cells across 5 annotated cell types. **Experimental design**: 2 donors, each contributing organoids to both control and VPA conditions (a paired design). Because we have only 2 biological replicates per condition, all differential expression results should be considered **exploratory**. **What this analysis covers**: 1. Visualization of cell populations (UMAP) 2. Cell type composition changes under VPA 3. Pseudobulk differential expression per cell type (limma-voom, paired design) 4. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA with Hallmark and GO gene sets) 5. Expression of known VPA-response and neural development genes ## Setup & Data Loading ```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false library(SingleCellExperiment) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(edgeR) library(limma) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(patchwork) library(DT) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggrepel) library(fgsea) library(msigdbr) library(pheatmap) library(scales) library(glue) library(here) library(Matrix) library(viridis) base_size <- 14 theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = base_size)) ``` ```{r} #| label: load-data sce <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "vpa_organoids_sce.rds")) # Map Ensembl IDs to gene symbols where available # feature_name contains gene symbols for annotated genes, ENSG IDs otherwise gene_symbols <- as.character(rowData(sce)$feature_name) is_symbol <- !grepl("^ENSG", gene_symbols) # Make symbols unique (some may be duplicated) symbol_map <- gene_symbols symbol_map[is_symbol] <- make.unique(symbol_map[is_symbol]) names(symbol_map) <- rownames(sce) # Create a lookup from ENSG to symbol ensg_to_symbol <- setNames(gene_symbols, rownames(sce)) # Rename rows to gene symbols where available rownames(sce) <- symbol_map ``` The dataset contains **`r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells** and **`r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes** (`r sum(is_symbol)` with gene symbols, `r sum(!is_symbol)` Ensembl IDs only). ```{r} #| label: color-palettes cell_type_colors <- c( "progenitor cell" = "#1b9e77", "neuronal-restricted precursor" = "#d95f02", "cerebral cortex neuron" = "#7570b3", "Cajal-Retzius cell" = "#e7298a", "unknown" = "#999999" ) condition_colors <- c( "CTRL" = "#4393c3", "VPA" = "#d6604d" ) donor_colors <- c( "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62" ) names(donor_colors) <- sort(unique(sce$donor_id)) ``` ```{r} #| label: gene-link-helper #' Create a clickable GeneCards link for a gene symbol gene_link <- function(symbol) { paste0( '', symbol, '' ) } ``` ## Experimental Design Overview The experiment uses a **paired design**: each donor contributes cells to both conditions. This lets us account for donor-to-donor variability when testing for VPA effects. ```{r} #| label: design-tables knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)), caption = "Cells per condition × donor" ) knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$cell_type)), caption = "Cells per condition × cell type" ) ``` ```{r} #| label: design-table-dt design_df <- as.data.frame( table( Condition = sce$condition, Donor = sce$donor_id, CellType = sce$cell_type ) ) |> dplyr::filter(Freq > 0) |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = Condition, values_from = Freq, values_fill = 0 ) DT::datatable( design_df, caption = "Cell counts by donor, condition, and cell type", options = list(pageLength = 20) ) ``` ## UMAP Visualizations UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D for visualization. Cells that are close together on the UMAP have similar expression profiles. The UMAP coordinates here were computed by the original study authors. ```{r} #| label: umap-data umap_df <- data.frame( UMAP1 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 1], UMAP2 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 2], cell_type = sce$cell_type, condition = sce$condition, donor_id = sce$donor_id, cell_phase = sce$cell_phase ) ``` ### UMAP by Cell Type ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-type #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell type", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-condition #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = condition)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = condition_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = Differential Expression Analysis ### Pseudobulk Aggregation Single-cell DE analysis requires careful statistical treatment. Simply treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates false positives because cells from the same donor are correlated. The **pseudobulk** approach addresses this by summing expression counts across all cells of a given type within each biological replicate (donor × condition), then applying bulk RNA-seq statistical methods. Since the CELLxGENE data provides log1p-normalized values rather than raw counts, we back-transform with `expm1()` and round to approximate integer counts. This is a standard workaround and the pseudobulk summation over thousands of cells smooths rounding artifacts. ```{r} #| label: pseudobulk-aggregation #| message: false # Back-transform log1p to approximate counts # Work per cell type to manage memory cell_types_for_de <- c( "progenitor cell", "cerebral cortex neuron", "neuronal-restricted precursor" ) # Create pseudobulk samples make_pseudobulk <- function(sce, cell_type_name) { idx <- which(sce$cell_type == cell_type_name) sub <- sce[, idx] # Define groups groups <- paste(sub$condition, sub$donor_id, sep = "_") group_levels <- unique(groups) # Sum approximate counts per group mat <- assay(sub, "X") n_genes <- nrow(mat) pb <- matrix(0, nrow = n_genes, ncol = length(group_levels), dimnames = list(rownames(mat), group_levels)) for (i in seq_along(group_levels)) { g <- group_levels[i] cells <- which(groups == g) if (length(cells) == 1) { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(round(expm1(mat[, cells]))) } else { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(Matrix::rowSums(round(expm1(mat[, cells, drop = FALSE])))) } } # Sample metadata sample_info <- data.frame( sample = group_levels, condition = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_.*$", "\\1", group_levels), donor_id = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_", "", group_levels), n_cells = as.integer(table(groups)[group_levels]), row.names = group_levels ) list(counts = as.matrix(pb), sample_info = sample_info) } pseudobulk_list <- lapply( setNames(cell_types_for_de, cell_types_for_de), function(ct) make_pseudobulk(sce, ct) ) # Show sample sizes pb_sample_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { info <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]]$sample_info[, c("sample", "condition", "n_cells")] info$cell_type <- ct info })) knitr::kable( pb_sample_info[, c("cell_type", "sample", "condition", "n_cells")], caption = "Pseudobulk sample sizes", row.names = FALSE ) ``` ### limma-voom Differential Expression We use **limma-voom** with a paired design formula `~donor_id + condition` to test for VPA effects while blocking on donor variability. The **empirical Bayes** shrinkage in limma is especially valuable with small sample sizes, as it borrows information across genes to stabilize variance estimates. **Important caveat**: With only 2 donors per condition, statistical power is limited. These results identify candidate genes for follow-up but should not be treated as definitive. ```{r} #| label: limma-voom-de #| message: false #| warning: false run_limma_voom <- function(pb, cell_type_name) { counts <- pb$counts info <- pb$sample_info # Create DGEList y <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = info) # Filter lowly expressed genes keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition) y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # Normalize y <- calcNormFactors(y) # Design matrix (paired) design <- model.matrix(~donor_id + condition, data = info) # voom transformation v <- voom(y, design, plot = FALSE) # Fit fit <- lmFit(v, design) fit <- eBayes(fit) # Extract results for VPA effect # The coefficient name depends on the factor levels coef_name <- grep("condition", colnames(coef(fit)), value = TRUE) tt <- topTable(fit, coef = coef_name, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt$cell_type <- cell_type_name tt } de_results <- lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { run_limma_voom(pseudobulk_list[[ct]], ct) }) names(de_results) <- names(pseudobulk_list) de_all <- bind_rows(de_results) ``` ### DE Summary ```{r} #| label: de-summary de_summary <- de_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> summarize( genes_tested = n(), up_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), up_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) DT::datatable(de_summary, caption = "Number of DE genes per cell type (VPA vs CTRL)", options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ### Volcano Plots Volcano plots show the relationship between effect size (log fold change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis). Genes in the upper corners are both large in effect and statistically significant. ```{r} #| label: volcano-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 6 #| warning: false volcano_plots <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] df$sig <- ifelse(df$adj.P.Val < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "NS") # Top genes to label top_genes <- df |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> head(15) ggplot(df, aes(logFC, -log10(adj.P.Val), color = sig)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("FDR < 0.05" = "red", "NS" = "grey60")) + geom_text_repel( data = top_genes, aes(label = gene), size = 0.9 * base_size / ggplot2::.pt, max.overlaps = 20, color = "black" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") + labs( title = ct, x = "log2 Fold Change (VPA vs CTRL)", y = "-log10(adj. P-value)", color = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") }) wrap_plots(volcano_plots, nrow = 1) ``` ### Top DE Genes Table ```{r} #| label: de-table #| warning: false # DT warns about data size due to embedded HTML gene links; harmless top_de <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> mutate( gene = gene_link(gene), logFC = round(logFC, 3), AveExpr = round(AveExpr, 2), t = round(t, 2), P.Value = signif(P.Value, 3), adj.P.Val = signif(adj.P.Val, 3), B = round(B, 2) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, gene, logFC, AveExpr, t, P.Value, adj.P.Val, B) DT::datatable( top_de, caption = "DE genes (FDR < 0.10) across cell types — click gene name for GeneCards", escape = FALSE, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(5, "asc"))) ) ``` ### Heatmap of Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: de-heatmap #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 10 # Get top DE genes across all cell types top_genes_for_heatmap <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> slice_head(n = 25) |> ungroup() |> pull(gene) |> unique() if (length(top_genes_for_heatmap) > 2) { # Build a matrix of logFC values across pseudobulk samples # Use the averaged log-CPM from each pseudobulk heatmap_data <- list() for (ct in names(pseudobulk_list)) { pb <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]] y <- DGEList(counts = pb$counts, samples = pb$sample_info) y <- calcNormFactors(y) lcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE) genes_avail <- intersect(top_genes_for_heatmap, rownames(lcpm)) if (length(genes_avail) > 0) { mat <- lcpm[genes_avail, , drop = FALSE] colnames(mat) <- paste0(ct, ":", colnames(mat)) heatmap_data[[ct]] <- mat } } # Combine and scale all_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(heatmap_data, rownames)) if (length(all_genes) > 2) { hm_mat <- do.call(cbind, lapply(heatmap_data, function(m) m[all_genes, ])) hm_scaled <- t(scale(t(hm_mat))) # Annotation ann_col <- data.frame( condition = sub(".*:(CTRL|VPA)_.*", "\\1", colnames(hm_mat)), cell_type = sub(":.*", "", colnames(hm_mat)), row.names = colnames(hm_mat) ) pheatmap( hm_scaled, annotation_col = ann_col, show_rownames = (nrow(hm_scaled) <= 50), cluster_cols = TRUE, cluster_rows = TRUE, main = "Top DE genes across pseudobulk samples (z-scored log-CPM)", fontsize_row = 7 ) } else { cat("Too few shared DE genes across cell types for a meaningful heatmap.\n") } } else { cat("Fewer than 3 DE genes at FDR < 0.10; skipping heatmap.\n") } ``` ## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether genes belonging to known biological pathways are systematically shifted up or down in expression. Rather than testing one gene at a time, GSEA tests **sets of genes** that share a function, making it more sensitive to coordinated but modest changes. We rank genes by their limma t-statistic (which captures both effect size and certainty) and test against **Hallmark** and **GO Biological Process** gene sets from MSigDB. ```{r} #| label: gsea-gene-sets #| message: false # Get gene sets hallmark_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) hallmark <- split(hallmark_df$gene_symbol, hallmark_df$gs_name) gobp_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) gobp <- split(gobp_df$gene_symbol, gobp_df$gs_name) # Combine all_gene_sets <- c(hallmark, gobp) ``` ```{r} #| label: gsea-run #| message: false #| warning: false gsea_results <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] # Create ranked list by t-statistic ranks <- setNames(df$t, df$gene) ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) # Run fgsea res <- fgsea( pathways = all_gene_sets, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500 ) res$cell_type <- ct res }) names(gsea_results) <- names(de_results) gsea_all <- bind_rows(gsea_results) ``` ### Top Enriched Pathways ```{r} #| label: gsea-dotplot #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 14 < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(padj)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } else { cat("No pathways reached significance at padj < 0.05.\n") # Show top pathways at a relaxed threshold top_pathways_relaxed <- gsea_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(pval) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways_relaxed) > 0) { top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub( "^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway ) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways_relaxed, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(pval), color = NES )) + The use of back-transformed log1p data rather than raw counts introduces approximation, though pseudobulk aggregation mitigates this. ## Draft Methods ### Data Source Single-cell RNA-seq data were obtained from CELLxGENE (dataset ID: `3a8aec06-3309-4d37-b75d-c59f5f6d55a6`), originating from Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv). The dataset comprises human dorsal forebrain organoids from `r n_donors` donors under control and VPA-treated conditions (`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells total). ### Preprocessing Data were provided as log1p-normalized expression values. UMAP coordinates and cell type annotations from the original authors were used without modification. ### Differential Expression Pseudobulk expression profiles were generated by summing back-transformed (expm1) approximate counts per gene across cells within each donor × condition × cell type group. Differential expression was performed using the limma-voom pipeline (Ritchie et al. 2015) with a paired design formula (~donor_id + condition). Genes were filtered using `filterByExpr()`, library sizes normalized with TMM (`calcNormFactors()`), and precision weights estimated via `voom()`. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied with `eBayes()`. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. ### Pathway Analysis Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea (Korotkevich et al. 2021) with genes ranked by limma t-statistic. MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets were tested (gene set sizes 15–500). ### Software ```{r} #| label: methods-software #| echo: false #| results: asis pkgs <- c("R", "SingleCellExperiment", "edgeR", "limma", "fgsea", "msigdbr", "ggplot2", "plotly") versions <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) { if (p == "R") { paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".") } else { as.character(packageVersion(p)) } }) cat(paste( paste0("**", pkgs, "** v", versions), collapse = ", " ), "\n") ``` ## References - Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK (2015). --- title: "Control vs VPA-Treated Dorsal Forebrain Organoids: scRNA-seq Analysis" author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)" date: now date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm" format: html: page-layout: full embed-resources: true toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" include-in-header: text: | --- ## Introduction Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug that also acts as a **histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor**. Prenatal exposure to VPA is an established teratogen and has been linked to increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental conditions. This analysis examines single-cell RNA-seq data from [Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632137), comparing **control** vs **VPA-treated** human dorsal forebrain organoids. The dataset was obtained from [CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) and contains 26,499 cells across 5 annotated cell types. **Experimental design**: 2 donors, each contributing organoids to both control and VPA conditions (a paired design). Because we have only 2 biological replicates per condition, all differential expression results should be considered **exploratory**. **What this analysis covers**: 1. Visualization of cell populations (UMAP) 2. Cell type composition changes under VPA 3. Pseudobulk differential expression per cell type (limma-voom, paired design) 4. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA with Hallmark and GO gene sets) 5. Expression of known VPA-response and neural development genes ## Setup & Data Loading ```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false library(SingleCellExperiment) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(edgeR) library(limma) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(patchwork) library(DT) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggrepel) library(fgsea) library(msigdbr) library(pheatmap) library(scales) library(glue) library(here) library(Matrix) library(viridis) base_size <- 14 theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = base_size)) ``` ```{r} #| label: load-data sce <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "vpa_organoids_sce.rds")) # Map Ensembl IDs to gene symbols where available # feature_name contains gene symbols for annotated genes, ENSG IDs otherwise gene_symbols <- as.character(rowData(sce)$feature_name) is_symbol <- !grepl("^ENSG", gene_symbols) # Make symbols unique (some may be duplicated) symbol_map <- gene_symbols symbol_map[is_symbol] <- make.unique(symbol_map[is_symbol]) names(symbol_map) <- rownames(sce) # Create a lookup from ENSG to symbol ensg_to_symbol <- setNames(gene_symbols, rownames(sce)) # Rename rows to gene symbols where available rownames(sce) <- symbol_map ``` The dataset contains **`r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells** and **`r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes** (`r sum(is_symbol)` with gene symbols, `r sum(!is_symbol)` Ensembl IDs only). ```{r} #| label: color-palettes cell_type_colors <- c( "progenitor cell" = "#1b9e77", "neuronal-restricted precursor" = "#d95f02", "cerebral cortex neuron" = "#7570b3", "Cajal-Retzius cell" = "#e7298a", "unknown" = "#999999" ) condition_colors <- c( "CTRL" = "#4393c3", "VPA" = "#d6604d" ) donor_colors <- c( "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62" ) names(donor_colors) <- sort(unique(sce$donor_id)) ``` ```{r} #| label: gene-link-helper #' Create a clickable GeneCards link for a gene symbol gene_link <- function(symbol) { paste0( '', symbol, '' ) } ``` ## Experimental Design Overview The experiment uses a **paired design**: each donor contributes cells to both conditions. This lets us account for donor-to-donor variability when testing for VPA effects. ```{r} #| label: design-tables knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)), caption = "Cells per condition × donor" ) knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$cell_type)), caption = "Cells per condition × cell type" ) ``` ```{r} #| label: design-table-dt design_df <- as.data.frame( table( Condition = sce$condition, Donor = sce$donor_id, CellType = sce$cell_type ) ) |> dplyr::filter(Freq > 0) |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = Condition, values_from = Freq, values_fill = 0 ) DT::datatable( design_df, caption = "Cell counts by donor, condition, and cell type", options = list(pageLength = 20) ) ``` ## UMAP Visualizations UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D for visualization. Cells that are close together on the UMAP have similar expression profiles. The UMAP coordinates here were computed by the original study authors. ```{r} #| label: umap-data umap_df <- data.frame( UMAP1 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 1], UMAP2 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 2], cell_type = sce$cell_type, condition = sce$condition, donor_id = sce$donor_id, cell_phase = sce$cell_phase ) ``` ### UMAP by Cell Type ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-type #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell type", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-condition #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = condition)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = condition_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by condition", color = "Condition") ``` ### UMAP Split by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-split-condition #| fig-width: 14 #| fig-height: 6 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + facet_wrap(~condition) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP split by condition", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Donor ```{r} #| label: umap-donor #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = donor_id)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = donor_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by donor", color = "Donor") ``` ### UMAP by Cell Cycle Phase ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-phase #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_phase)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell cycle phase", color = "Cell phase") ``` ### Interactive UMAP (Plotly) :::{.column-screen} ```{r} #| label: umap-plotly #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 7 # Subsample for plotly performance set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(umap_df), min(10000, nrow(umap_df))) umap_sub <- umap_df[idx, ] p <- plot_ly( umap_sub, x = ~UMAP1, y = ~UMAP2, color = ~cell_type, colors = cell_type_colors, text = ~ paste( "Cell type:", cell_type, "
Condition:", condition, "
Donor:", donor_id ), type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.6), width = 900, height = 650 ) |> layout( title = "Interactive UMAP (10,000 cell subsample)", xaxis = list(title = "UMAP1"), yaxis = list(title = "UMAP2") ) p `` ` ::: ## Cell Type Composition Analysis A key question in case-control scRNA-seq studies is whether the **proportions** of cell types shift between conditions. Changes in composition can reflect altered differentiation, proliferation, or survival. ```{r} #| label: composition-data comp_df <- as.data.frame(table( condition = sce$condition, cell_type = sce$cell_type, donor_id = sce$donor_id )) # Compute proportions within each condition × donor comp_df <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, donor_id) |> mutate( total = sum(Freq), proportion = Freq / total ) |> ungroup() ``` ### Stacked Bar Chart ```{r} #| label: composition-stacked #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 6 # Per condition (aggregated across donors) comp_cond <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, cell_type) |> summarize(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |> group_by(condition) |> mutate(proportion = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> ungroup() ggplot(comp_cond, aes(condition, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition", x = "Condition", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition by Donor ```{r} #| label: composition-by-donor #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 6 comp_df$sample <- paste(comp_df$condition, comp_df$donor_id, sep = "\n") ggplot(comp_df, aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition and donor", x = "Sample", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition Table ```{r} #| label: composition-table comp_table <- comp_cond |> mutate( label = paste0(Freq, " (", round(proportion * 100, 1), "%)") ) |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, label) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = label) DT::datatable(comp_table, caption = "Cell counts and proportions per condition", escape = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ## Differential Expression Analysis ### Pseudobulk Aggregation Single-cell DE analysis requires careful statistical treatment. Simply treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates false positives because cells from the same donor are correlated. The **pseudobulk** approach addresses this by summing expression counts across all cells of a given type within each biological replicate (donor × condition), then applying bulk RNA-seq statistical methods. Since the CELLxGENE data provides log1p-normalized values rather than raw counts, we back-transform with `expm1()` and round to approximate integer counts. This is a standard workaround and the pseudobulk summation over thousands of cells smooths rounding artifacts. ```{r} #| label: pseudobulk-aggregation #| message: false # Back-transform log1p to approximate counts # Work per cell type to manage memory cell_types_for_de <- c( "progenitor cell", "cerebral cortex neuron", "neuronal-restricted precursor" ) # Create pseudobulk samples make_pseudobulk <- function(sce, cell_type_name) { idx <- which(sce$cell_type == cell_type_name) sub <- sce[, idx] # Define groups groups <- paste(sub$condition, sub$donor_id, sep = "_") group_levels <- unique(groups) # Sum approximate counts per group mat <- assay(sub, "X") n_genes <- nrow(mat) pb <- matrix(0, nrow = n_genes, ncol = length(group_levels), dimnames = list(rownames(mat), group_levels)) for (i in seq_along(group_levels)) { g <- group_levels[i] cells <- which(groups == g) if (length(cells) == 1) { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(round(expm1(mat[, cells]))) } else { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(Matrix::rowSums(round(expm1(mat[, cells, drop = FALSE])))) } } # Sample metadata sample_info <- data.frame( sample = group_levels, condition = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_.*$", "\\1", group_levels), donor_id = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_", "", group_levels), n_cells = as.integer(table(groups)[group_levels]), row.names = group_levels ) list(counts = as.matrix(pb), sample_info = sample_info) } pseudobulk_list <- lapply( setNames(cell_types_for_de, cell_types_for_de), function(ct) make_pseudobulk(sce, ct) ) # Show sample sizes pb_sample_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { info <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]]$sample_info[, c("sample", "condition", "n_cells")] info$cell_type <- ct info })) knitr::kable( pb_sample_info[, c("cell_type", "sample", "condition", "n_cells")], caption = "Pseudobulk sample sizes", row.names = FALSE ) ``` ### limma-voom Differential Expression We use **limma-voom** with a paired design formula `~donor_id + condition` to test for VPA effects while blocking on donor variability. The **empirical Bayes** shrinkage in limma is especially valuable with small sample sizes, as it borrows information across genes to stabilize variance estimates. **Important caveat**: With only 2 donors per condition, statistical power is limited. These results identify candidate genes for follow-up but should not be treated as definitive. ```{r} #| label: limma-voom-de #| message: false #| warning: false run_limma_voom <- function(pb, cell_type_name) { counts <- pb$counts info <- pb$sample_info # Create DGEList y <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = info) # Filter lowly expressed genes keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition) y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # Normalize y <- calcNormFactors(y) # Design matrix (paired) design <- model.matrix(~donor_id + condition, data = info) # voom transformation v <- voom(y, design, plot = FALSE) # Fit fit <- lmFit(v, design) fit <- eBayes(fit) # Extract results for VPA effect # The coefficient name depends on the factor levels coef_name <- grep("condition", colnames(coef(fit)), value = TRUE) tt <- topTable(fit, coef = coef_name, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt$cell_type <- cell_type_name tt } de_results <- lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { run_limma_voom(pseudobulk_list[[ct]], ct) }) names(de_results) <- names(pseudobulk_list) de_all <- bind_rows(de_results) ``` ### DE Summary ```{r} #| label: de-summary de_summary <- de_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> summarize( genes_tested = n(), up_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), up_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) DT::datatable(de_summary, caption = "Number of DE genes per cell type (VPA vs CTRL)", options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ### Volcano Plots Volcano plots show the relationship between effect size (log fold change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis). Genes in the upper corners are both large in effect and statistically significant. ```{r} #| label: volcano-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 6 #| warning: false volcano_plots <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] df$sig <- ifelse(df$adj.P.Val < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "NS") # Top genes to label top_genes <- df |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> head(15) ggplot(df, aes(logFC, -log10(adj.P.Val), color = sig)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("FDR < 0.05" = "red", "NS" = "grey60")) + geom_text_repel( data = top_genes, aes(label = gene), size = 0.9 * base_size / ggplot2::.pt, max.overlaps = 20, color = "black" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") + labs( title = ct, x = "log2 Fold Change (VPA vs CTRL)", y = "-log10(adj. P-value)", color = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") }) wrap_plots(volcano_plots, nrow = 1) ``` ### Top DE Genes Table ```{r} #| label: de-table #| warning: false # DT warns about data size due to embedded HTML gene links; harmless top_de <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> mutate( gene = gene_link(gene), logFC = round(logFC, 3), AveExpr = round(AveExpr, 2), t = round(t, 2), P.Value = signif(P.Value, 3), adj.P.Val = signif(adj.P.Val, 3), B = round(B, 2) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, gene, logFC, AveExpr, t, P.Value, adj.P.Val, B) DT::datatable( top_de, caption = "DE genes (FDR < 0.10) across cell types — click gene name for GeneCards", escape = FALSE, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(5, "asc"))) ) ``` ### Heatmap of Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: de-heatmap #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 10 # Get top DE genes across all cell types top_genes_for_heatmap <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> slice_head(n = 25) |> ungroup() |> pull(gene) |> unique() if (length(top_genes_for_heatmap) > 2) { # Build a matrix of logFC values across pseudobulk samples # Use the averaged log-CPM from each pseudobulk heatmap_data <- list() for (ct in names(pseudobulk_list)) { pb <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]] y <- DGEList(counts = pb$counts, samples = pb$sample_info) y <- calcNormFactors(y) lcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE) genes_avail <- intersect(top_genes_for_heatmap, rownames(lcpm)) if (length(genes_avail) > 0) { mat <- lcpm[genes_avail, , drop = FALSE] colnames(mat) <- paste0(ct, ":", colnames(mat)) heatmap_data[[ct]] <- mat } } # Combine and scale all_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(heatmap_data, rownames)) if (length(all_genes) > 2) { hm_mat <- do.call(cbind, lapply(heatmap_data, function(m) m[all_genes, ])) hm_scaled <- t(scale(t(hm_mat))) # Annotation ann_col <- data.frame( condition = sub(".*:(CTRL|VPA)_.*", "\\1", colnames(hm_mat)), cell_type = sub(":.*", "", colnames(hm_mat)), row.names = colnames(hm_mat) ) pheatmap( hm_scaled, annotation_col = ann_col, show_rownames = (nrow(hm_scaled) <= 50), cluster_cols = TRUE, cluster_rows = TRUE, main = "Top DE genes across pseudobulk samples (z-scored log-CPM)", fontsize_row = 7 ) } else { cat("Too few shared DE genes across cell types for a meaningful heatmap.\n") } } else { cat("Fewer than 3 DE genes at FDR < 0.10; skipping heatmap.\n") } ``` ## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether genes belonging to known biological pathways are systematically shifted up or down in expression. Rather than testing one gene at a time, GSEA tests **sets of genes** that share a function, making it more sensitive to coordinated but modest changes. We rank genes by their limma t-statistic (which captures both effect size and certainty) and test against **Hallmark** and **GO Biological Process** gene sets from MSigDB. ```{r} #| label: gsea-gene-sets #| message: false # Get gene sets hallmark_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) hallmark <- split(hallmark_df$gene_symbol, hallmark_df$gs_name) gobp_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) gobp <- split(gobp_df$gene_symbol, gobp_df$gs_name) # Combine all_gene_sets <- c(hallmark, gobp) ``` ```{r} #| label: gsea-run #| message: false #| warning: false gsea_results <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] # Create ranked list by t-statistic ranks <- setNames(df$t, df$gene) ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) # Run fgsea res <- fgsea( pathways = all_gene_sets, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500 ) res$cell_type <- ct res }) names(gsea_results) <- names(de_results) gsea_all <- bind_rows(gsea_results) ``` ### Top Enriched Pathways ```{r} #| label: gsea-dotplot #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 14 #| warning: false # Top pathways per cell type (by adjusted p-value) top_pathways <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(padj < 0.05) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(padj) |> slice_head(n = 15) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways) > 0) { # Clean names for display top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways$pathway) top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways$pathway_short) top_pathways$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(padj), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top enriched pathways (GSEA, padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(padj)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } else { cat("No pathways reached significance at padj < 0.05.\n") # Show top pathways at a relaxed threshold top_pathways_relaxed <- gsea_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(pval) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways_relaxed) > 0) { top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub( "^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway ) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways_relaxed, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(pval), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top pathways by nominal p-value (none reached padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(p-value)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } } ``` ### GSEA Results Table ```{r} #| label: gsea-table gsea_table <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(pval < 0.05) |> arrange(pval) |> mutate( NES = round(NES, 2), pval = signif(pval, 3), padj = signif(padj, 3), size = as.integer(size) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, pathway, NES, pval, padj, size) |> head(100) DT::datatable( gsea_table, caption = "GSEA results (nominal p < 0.05)", options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(3, "asc"))) ) ``` ## Known Biology Check We examine genes known to be responsive to VPA or involved in neural development to see whether their expression patterns are consistent with expectations. **Selected genes**: - **HDAC targets / chromatin remodeling**: *HDAC1*, *HDAC2*, *HDAC3*, *EP300*, *CREBBP* - **Neural progenitor markers**: *PAX6*, *SOX2*, *NES*, *HES1*, *NOTCH1* - **Neuronal differentiation**: *DCX*, *TBR1*, *NEUROD1*, *NEUROD2*, *MAP2* - **Cortical layer markers**: *SATB2*, *BCL11B* (CTIP2), *TLE4* - **Apoptosis / cell stress**: *TP53*, *BCL2*, *BAX* ```{r} #| label: known-genes-data known_genes <- c( "HDAC1", "HDAC2", "HDAC3", "EP300", "CREBBP", "PAX6", "SOX2", "NES", "HES1", "NOTCH1", "DCX", "TBR1", "NEUROD1", "NEUROD2", "MAP2", "SATB2", "BCL11B", "TLE4", length(known_genes), "\n") cat("Missing:", setdiff(known_genes, known_genes_present), "\n") ``` ### Violin Plots ```{r} #| label: known-genes-violin #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 10 #| warning: dplyr::filter(gene %in% gene_groups[[i]]) |> ggplot(aes(condition, expression, fill = condition)) + geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_manual(values = if (length(top_de_genes) < 4) { top_de_genes <- de_all |> arrange(P.Value) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) } if (length(top_de_genes) > 0) { # Extract expression expr_top <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[top_de_genes, , drop = FALSE]) umap_expr <- umap_df for (g in top_de_genes) { umap_expr[[g]] <- expr_top[g, ] } feature_plots <- lapply(top_de_genes, function(g) { ggplot(umap_expr[sample(nrow(umap_expr)), ], aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = .data[[g]])) + geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_viridis(option = "magma") + labs(title = g, color = "log1p\nexpr") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(0.5, "cm")) }) wrap_plots(feature_plots, ncol = 4) } ``` ## Draft Results ```{r} #| label: results-data #| echo: false n_cells <- ncol(sce) n_ctrl <- |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, proportion) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = proportion) |> mutate(change_pct = round((VPA - CTRL) * 100, 1)) # DE counts n_de_005 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) n_de_010 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE) # Top pathway top_pw <- gsea_all |> arrange(pval) |> head(1) ``` ### Results Summary We analyzed `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells from `r n_donors` donors across `r n_cell_types` cell types, comparing CTRL (`r format(n_ctrl, big.mark = ",")` cells) to VPA-treated (`r format(n_vpa, big.mark = ",")` cells) human dorsal forebrain organoids. **Cell type composition**: VPA treatment was associated with notable shifts in cell type proportions: ```{r} #| label: results-comp-table #| echo: false DT::datatable( comp_summary |> mutate( CTRL = paste0(round(CTRL * 100, 1), "%"), VPA = paste0(round(VPA * 100, 1), "%"), ` Change(pp) ` = change_pct ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, CTRL, VPA, ` Change(pp) `), caption = "Cell type proportion changes (percentage points)", options = list(dom = "t"), rownames = FALSE ) ``` **Differential expression**: Across the three major cell types tested, we identified `r n_de_005` genes at FDR < 0.05 and `r n_de_010` genes at FDR < 0.10. **Pathway enrichment**: The top enriched pathway was *`r gsub("_", " ", top_pw$pathway[1])`* in `r top_pw$cell_type[1]` (NES = `r round(top_pw$NES[1], 2)`, nominal p = `r signif(top_pw$pval[1], 3)`). **Limitations**: With only `r n_donors` donors per condition, these results are exploratory. The use of back-transformed log1p data rather than raw counts introduces approximation, though pseudobulk aggregation mitigates this. ## Draft Methods ### Data Source Single-cell RNA-seq data were obtained from CELLxGENE (dataset ID: `3a8aec06-3309-4d37-b75d-c59f5f6d55a6`), originating from Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv). The dataset comprises human dorsal forebrain organoids from `r n_donors` donors under control and VPA-treated conditions (`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells total). ### Preprocessing Data were provided as log1p-normalized expression values. UMAP coordinates and cell type annotations from the original authors were used without modification. ### Differential Expression Pseudobulk expression profiles were generated by summing back-transformed (expm1) approximate counts per gene across cells within each donor × condition × cell type group. Differential expression was performed using the limma-voom pipeline (Ritchie et al. 2015) with a paired design formula (~donor_id + condition). Genes were filtered using `filterByExpr()`, library sizes normalized with TMM (`calcNormFactors()`), and precision weights estimated via `voom()`. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied with `eBayes()`. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. ### Pathway Analysis Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea (Korotkevich et al. 2021) with genes ranked by limma t-statistic. MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets were tested (gene set sizes 15–500). ### Software ```{r} #| label: methods-software #| echo: false #| results: asis pkgs <- c("R", "SingleCellExperiment", "edgeR", "limma", "fgsea", "msigdbr", "ggplot2", "plotly") versions <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) { if (p == "R") { paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".") } else { as.character(packageVersion(p)) } }) cat(paste( paste0("**", pkgs, "** v", versions), collapse = ", " ), "\n") ``` ## References - Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK (2015).
