head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 0 (unlimited).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To read a directory, use an ls command via the Bash tool.
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively read multiple potentially useful files in parallel.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file. 
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: spaces + line number + tab. Everything after that tab is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem.

Usage:
- This tool will overwrite the existing file if there is one at the provided path.
- If this is an existing file, you MUST use the Read tool first to read the file's contents. This tool will fail if you did not read the file first.
- Prefer the Edit tool for modifying existing files — it only sends the diff. Only use this tool to create new files or for complete rewrites.
- NEVER create documentation files (*.md) or README files unless explicitly requested by the User.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid writing emojis to files unless asked.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Execute a skill within the main conversation

When users ask you to perform tasks, check if any of the available skills match. Skills provide specialized capabilities and domain knowledge.

When users reference a "slash command" or "/<something>" (e.g., "/commit", "/review-pr"), they are referring to a skill. Use this tool to invoke it.

How to invoke:
- Use this tool with the skill name and optional arguments
- Examples:
  - `skill: "pdf"` - invoke the pdf skill
  - `skill: "commit", args: "-m 'Fix bug'"` - invoke with arguments
  - `skill: "review-pr", args: "123"` - invoke with arguments
  - `skill: "ms-office-suite:pdf"` - invoke using fully qualified name

Important:
- Available skills are listed in system-reminder messages in the conversation
- When a skill matches the user's request, this is a BLOCKING REQUIREMENT: invoke the relevant Skill tool BEFORE generating any other response about the task
- NEVER mention a skill without actually calling this tool
- Do not invoke a skill that is already running
- Do not use this tool for built-in CLI commands (like /help, /clear, etc.)
- If you see a <command-name> tag in the current conversation turn, the skill has ALREADY been loaded - follow the instructions directly instead of calling this tool again

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <available-deferred-tools> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

messages.content:
--- title: "Control vs VPA-Treated Dorsal Forebrain Organoids: scRNA-seq Analysis" author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)" date: now date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm" format: html: page-layout: full embed-resources: true toc: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" include-in-header: text: | --- ## Introduction Valproic acid (VPA) is a widely prescribed antiepileptic drug that also acts as a **histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor**. Prenatal exposure to VPA is an established teratogen and has been linked to increased risk of autism spectrum disorder and other neurodevelopmental conditions. This analysis examines single-cell RNA-seq data from [Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv)](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.01.09.632137), comparing **control** vs **VPA-treated** human dorsal forebrain organoids. The dataset was obtained from [CELLxGENE](https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/) and contains 26,499 cells across 5 annotated cell types. **Experimental design**: 2 donors, each contributing organoids to both control and VPA conditions (a paired design). Because we have only 2 biological replicates per condition, all differential expression results should be considered **exploratory**. **What this analysis covers**: 1. Visualization of cell populations (UMAP) 2. Cell type composition changes under VPA 3. Pseudobulk differential expression per cell type (limma-voom, paired design) 4. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA with Hallmark and GO gene sets) 5. Expression of known VPA-response and neural development genes ## Setup & Data Loading ```{r} #| label: setup #| message: false #| warning: false library(SingleCellExperiment) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(edgeR) library(limma) library(ggplot2) library(plotly) library(patchwork) library(DT) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggrepel) library(fgsea) library(msigdbr) library(pheatmap) library(scales) library(glue) library(here) library(Matrix) library(viridis) base_size <- 14 theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = base_size)) ``` ```{r} #| label: load-data sce <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "vpa_organoids_sce.rds")) # Map Ensembl IDs to gene symbols where available # feature_name contains gene symbols for annotated genes, ENSG IDs otherwise gene_symbols <- as.character(rowData(sce)$feature_name) is_symbol <- !grepl("^ENSG", gene_symbols) # Make symbols unique (some may be duplicated) symbol_map <- gene_symbols symbol_map[is_symbol] <- make.unique(symbol_map[is_symbol]) names(symbol_map) <- rownames(sce) # Create a lookup from ENSG to symbol ensg_to_symbol <- setNames(gene_symbols, rownames(sce)) # Rename rows to gene symbols where available rownames(sce) <- symbol_map ``` The dataset contains **`r format(ncol(sce), big.mark = ",")` cells** and **`r format(nrow(sce), big.mark = ",")` genes** (`r sum(is_symbol)` with gene symbols, `r sum(!is_symbol)` Ensembl IDs only). ```{r} #| label: color-palettes cell_type_colors <- c( "progenitor cell" = "#1b9e77", "neuronal-restricted precursor" = "#d95f02", "cerebral cortex neuron" = "#7570b3", "Cajal-Retzius cell" = "#e7298a", "unknown" = "#999999" ) condition_colors <- c( "CTRL" = "#4393c3", "VPA" = "#d6604d" ) donor_colors <- c( "#66c2a5", "#fc8d62" ) names(donor_colors) <- sort(unique(sce$donor_id)) ``` ```{r} #| label: gene-link-helper #' Create a clickable GeneCards link for a gene symbol gene_link <- function(symbol) { paste0( '', symbol, '' ) } ``` ## Experimental Design Overview The experiment uses a **paired design**: each donor contributes cells to both conditions. This lets us account for donor-to-donor variability when testing for VPA effects. ```{r} #| label: design-tables knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)), caption = "Cells per condition × donor" ) knitr::kable( as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$cell_type)), caption = "Cells per condition × cell type" ) ``` ```{r} #| label: design-table-dt design_df <- as.data.frame( table( Condition = sce$condition, Donor = sce$donor_id, CellType = sce$cell_type ) ) |> dplyr::filter(Freq > 0) |> tidyr::pivot_wider( names_from = Condition, values_from = Freq, values_fill = 0 ) DT::datatable( design_df, caption = "Cell counts by donor, condition, and cell type", options = list(pageLength = 20) ) ``` ## UMAP Visualizations UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimensionality reduction technique that projects high-dimensional gene expression data into 2D for visualization. Cells that are close together on the UMAP have similar expression profiles. The UMAP coordinates here were computed by the original study authors. ```{r} #| label: umap-data umap_df <- data.frame( UMAP1 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 1], UMAP2 = reducedDim(sce, "X_umap")[, 2], cell_type = sce$cell_type, condition = sce$condition, donor_id = sce$donor_id, cell_phase = sce$cell_phase ) ``` ### UMAP by Cell Type ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-type #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell type", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-condition #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = condition)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = condition_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by condition", color = "Condition") ``` ### UMAP Split by Condition ```{r} #| label: umap-split-condition #| fig-width: 14 #| fig-height: 6 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_type)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + facet_wrap(~condition) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP split by condition", color = "Cell type") ``` ### UMAP by Donor ```{r} #| label: umap-donor #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = donor_id)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + scale_color_manual(values = donor_colors) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by donor", color = "Donor") ``` ### UMAP by Cell Cycle Phase ```{r} #| label: umap-cell-phase #| fig-width: 9 #| fig-height: 7 ggplot(umap_df, aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = cell_phase)) + geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.4) + guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1))) + labs(title = "UMAP colored by cell cycle phase", color = "Cell phase") ``` ### Interactive UMAP (Plotly) :::{.column-screen} ```{r} #| label: umap-plotly #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 7 # Subsample for plotly performance set.seed(42) idx <- sample(nrow(umap_df), min(10000, nrow(umap_df))) umap_sub <- umap_df[idx, ] p <- plot_ly( umap_sub, x = ~UMAP1, y = ~UMAP2, color = ~cell_type, colors = cell_type_colors, text = ~ paste( "Cell type:", cell_type, "
Condition:", condition, "
Donor:", donor_id ), type = "scatter", mode = "markers", marker = list(size = 3, opacity = 0.6), width = 900, height = 650 ) |> layout( title = "Interactive UMAP (10,000 cell subsample)", xaxis = list(title = "UMAP1"), yaxis = list(title = "UMAP2") ) p `` ` ::: ## Cell Type Composition Analysis A key question in case-control scRNA-seq studies is whether the **proportions** of cell types shift between conditions. Changes in composition can reflect altered differentiation, proliferation, or survival. ```{r} #| label: composition-data comp_df <- as.data.frame(table( condition = sce$condition, cell_type = sce$cell_type, donor_id = sce$donor_id )) # Compute proportions within each condition × donor comp_df <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, donor_id) |> mutate( total = sum(Freq), proportion = Freq / total ) |> ungroup() ``` ### Stacked Bar Chart ```{r} #| label: composition-stacked #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 6 # Per condition (aggregated across donors) comp_cond <- comp_df |> group_by(condition, cell_type) |> summarize(Freq = sum(Freq), .groups = "drop") |> group_by(condition) |> mutate(proportion = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> ungroup() ggplot(comp_cond, aes(condition, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition", x = "Condition", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition by Donor ```{r} #| label: composition-by-donor #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 6 comp_df$sample <- paste(comp_df$condition, comp_df$donor_id, sep = "\n") ggplot(comp_df, aes(sample, proportion, fill = cell_type)) + geom_col(width = 0.6) + scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colors) + scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) + labs( title = "Cell type composition by condition and donor", x = "Sample", y = "Proportion", fill = "Cell type" ) ``` ### Composition Table ```{r} #| label: composition-table comp_table <- comp_cond |> mutate( label = paste0(Freq, " (", round(proportion * 100, 1), "%)") ) |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, label) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = label) DT::datatable(comp_table, caption = "Cell counts and proportions per condition", escape = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ## Differential Expression Analysis ### Pseudobulk Aggregation Single-cell DE analysis requires careful statistical treatment. Simply treating each cell as an independent replicate inflates false positives because cells from the same donor are correlated. The **pseudobulk** approach addresses this by summing expression counts across all cells of a given type within each biological replicate (donor × condition), then applying bulk RNA-seq statistical methods. Since the CELLxGENE data provides log1p-normalized values rather than raw counts, we back-transform with `expm1()` and round to approximate integer counts. This is a standard workaround and the pseudobulk summation over thousands of cells smooths rounding artifacts. ```{r} #| label: pseudobulk-aggregation #| message: false # Back-transform log1p to approximate counts # Work per cell type to manage memory cell_types_for_de <- c( "progenitor cell", "cerebral cortex neuron", "neuronal-restricted precursor" ) # Create pseudobulk samples make_pseudobulk <- function(sce, cell_type_name) { idx <- which(sce$cell_type == cell_type_name) sub <- sce[, idx] # Define groups groups <- paste(sub$condition, sub$donor_id, sep = "_") group_levels <- unique(groups) # Sum approximate counts per group mat <- assay(sub, "X") n_genes <- nrow(mat) pb <- matrix(0, nrow = n_genes, ncol = length(group_levels), dimnames = list(rownames(mat), group_levels)) for (i in seq_along(group_levels)) { g <- group_levels[i] cells <- which(groups == g) if (length(cells) == 1) { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(round(expm1(mat[, cells]))) } else { pb[, i] <- as.numeric(Matrix::rowSums(round(expm1(mat[, cells, drop = FALSE])))) } } # Sample metadata sample_info <- data.frame( sample = group_levels, condition = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_.*$", "\\1", group_levels), donor_id = sub("^(CTRL|VPA)_", "", group_levels), n_cells = as.integer(table(groups)[group_levels]), row.names = group_levels ) list(counts = as.matrix(pb), sample_info = sample_info) } pseudobulk_list <- lapply( setNames(cell_types_for_de, cell_types_for_de), function(ct) make_pseudobulk(sce, ct) ) # Show sample sizes pb_sample_info <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { info <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]]$sample_info[, c("sample", "condition", "n_cells")] info$cell_type <- ct info })) knitr::kable( pb_sample_info[, c("cell_type", "sample", "condition", "n_cells")], caption = "Pseudobulk sample sizes", row.names = FALSE ) ``` ### limma-voom Differential Expression We use **limma-voom** with a paired design formula `~donor_id + condition` to test for VPA effects while blocking on donor variability. The **empirical Bayes** shrinkage in limma is especially valuable with small sample sizes, as it borrows information across genes to stabilize variance estimates. **Important caveat**: With only 2 donors per condition, statistical power is limited. These results identify candidate genes for follow-up but should not be treated as definitive. ```{r} #| label: limma-voom-de #| message: false #| warning: false run_limma_voom <- function(pb, cell_type_name) { counts <- pb$counts info <- pb$sample_info # Create DGEList y <- DGEList(counts = counts, samples = info) # Filter lowly expressed genes keep <- filterByExpr(y, group = info$condition) y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE] # Normalize y <- calcNormFactors(y) # Design matrix (paired) design <- model.matrix(~donor_id + condition, data = info) # voom transformation v <- voom(y, design, plot = FALSE) # Fit fit <- lmFit(v, design) fit <- eBayes(fit) # Extract results for VPA effect # The coefficient name depends on the factor levels coef_name <- grep("condition", colnames(coef(fit)), value = TRUE) tt <- topTable(fit, coef = coef_name, number = Inf, sort.by = "none") tt$gene <- rownames(tt) tt$cell_type <- cell_type_name tt } de_results <- lapply(names(pseudobulk_list), function(ct) { run_limma_voom(pseudobulk_list[[ct]], ct) }) names(de_results) <- names(pseudobulk_list) de_all <- bind_rows(de_results) ``` ### DE Summary ```{r} #| label: de-summary de_summary <- de_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> summarize( genes_tested = n(), up_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR05 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.05 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), up_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC > 0, na.rm = TRUE), down_FDR10 = sum(adj.P.Val < 0.10 & logFC < 0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) DT::datatable(de_summary, caption = "Number of DE genes per cell type (VPA vs CTRL)", options = list(dom = "t")) ``` ### Volcano Plots Volcano plots show the relationship between effect size (log fold change, x-axis) and statistical significance (−log10 adjusted p-value, y-axis). Genes in the upper corners are both large in effect and statistically significant. ```{r} #| label: volcano-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 6 #| warning: false volcano_plots <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] df$sig <- ifelse(df$adj.P.Val < 0.05, "FDR < 0.05", "NS") # Top genes to label top_genes <- df |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.05) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> head(15) ggplot(df, aes(logFC, -log10(adj.P.Val), color = sig)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("FDR < 0.05" = "red", "NS" = "grey60")) + geom_text_repel( data = top_genes, aes(label = gene), size = 0.9 * base_size / ggplot2::.pt, max.overlaps = 20, color = "black" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") + labs( title = ct, x = "log2 Fold Change (VPA vs CTRL)", y = "-log10(adj. P-value)", color = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") }) wrap_plots(volcano_plots, nrow = 1) ``` ### Top DE Genes Table ```{r} #| label: de-table #| warning: false # DT warns about data size due to embedded HTML gene links; harmless top_de <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> mutate( gene = gene_link(gene), logFC = round(logFC, 3), AveExpr = round(AveExpr, 2), t = round(t, 2), P.Value = signif(P.Value, 3), adj.P.Val = signif(adj.P.Val, 3), B = round(B, 2) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, gene, logFC, AveExpr, t, P.Value, adj.P.Val, B) DT::datatable( top_de, caption = "DE genes (FDR < 0.10) across cell types — click gene name for GeneCards", escape = FALSE, rownames = FALSE, options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(5, "asc"))) ) ``` ### Heatmap of Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: de-heatmap #| fig-width: 12 #| fig-height: 10 # Get top DE genes across all cell types top_genes_for_heatmap <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> slice_head(n = 25) |> ungroup() |> pull(gene) |> unique() if (length(top_genes_for_heatmap) > 2) { # Build a matrix of logFC values across pseudobulk samples # Use the averaged log-CPM from each pseudobulk heatmap_data <- list() for (ct in names(pseudobulk_list)) { pb <- pseudobulk_list[[ct]] y <- DGEList(counts = pb$counts, samples = pb$sample_info) y <- calcNormFactors(y) lcpm <- cpm(y, log = TRUE) genes_avail <- intersect(top_genes_for_heatmap, rownames(lcpm)) if (length(genes_avail) > 0) { mat <- lcpm[genes_avail, , drop = FALSE] colnames(mat) <- paste0(ct, ":", colnames(mat)) heatmap_data[[ct]] <- mat } } # Combine and scale all_genes <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(heatmap_data, rownames)) if (length(all_genes) > 2) { hm_mat <- do.call(cbind, lapply(heatmap_data, function(m) m[all_genes, ])) hm_scaled <- t(scale(t(hm_mat))) # Annotation ann_col <- data.frame( condition = sub(".*:(CTRL|VPA)_.*", "\\1", colnames(hm_mat)), cell_type = sub(":.*", "", colnames(hm_mat)), row.names = colnames(hm_mat) ) pheatmap( hm_scaled, annotation_col = ann_col, show_rownames = (nrow(hm_scaled) <= 50), cluster_cols = TRUE, cluster_rows = TRUE, main = "Top DE genes across pseudobulk samples (z-scored log-CPM)", fontsize_row = 7 ) } else { cat("Too few shared DE genes across cell types for a meaningful heatmap.\n") } } else { cat("Fewer than 3 DE genes at FDR < 0.10; skipping heatmap.\n") } ``` ## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) asks whether genes belonging to known biological pathways are systematically shifted up or down in expression. Rather than testing one gene at a time, GSEA tests **sets of genes** that share a function, making it more sensitive to coordinated but modest changes. We rank genes by their limma t-statistic (which captures both effect size and certainty) and test against **Hallmark** and **GO Biological Process** gene sets from MSigDB. ```{r} #| label: gsea-gene-sets #| message: false # Get gene sets hallmark_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) hallmark <- split(hallmark_df$gene_symbol, hallmark_df$gs_name) gobp_df <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "C5", subcollection = "GO:BP") |> dplyr::select(gs_name, gene_symbol) gobp <- split(gobp_df$gene_symbol, gobp_df$gs_name) # Combine all_gene_sets <- c(hallmark, gobp) ``` ```{r} #| label: gsea-run #| message: false #| warning: false gsea_results <- lapply(names(de_results), function(ct) { df <- de_results[[ct]] # Create ranked list by t-statistic ranks <- setNames(df$t, df$gene) ranks <- sort(ranks, decreasing = TRUE) # Run fgsea res <- fgsea( pathways = all_gene_sets, stats = ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500 ) res$cell_type <- ct res }) names(gsea_results) <- names(de_results) gsea_all <- bind_rows(gsea_results) ``` ### Top Enriched Pathways ```{r} #| label: gsea-dotplot #| fig-width: 10 #| fig-height: 14 #| warning: false # Top pathways per cell type (by adjusted p-value) top_pathways <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(padj < 0.05) |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(padj) |> slice_head(n = 15) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways) > 0) { # Clean names for display top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways$pathway) top_pathways$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways$pathway_short) top_pathways$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(padj), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top enriched pathways (GSEA, padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(padj)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } else { cat("No pathways reached significance at padj < 0.05.\n") # Show top pathways at a relaxed threshold top_pathways_relaxed <- gsea_all |> group_by(cell_type) |> arrange(pval) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> ungroup() if (nrow(top_pathways_relaxed) > 0) { top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub( "^HALLMARK_|^GOBP_", "", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway ) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- gsub("_", " ", top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short <- tolower(top_pathways_relaxed$pathway_short) ggplot(top_pathways_relaxed, aes( x = NES, y = reorder(pathway_short, NES), size = -log10(pval), color = NES )) + geom_point() + scale_color_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "grey80", high = "red", midpoint = 0) + facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) + labs( title = "Top pathways by nominal p-value (none reached padj < 0.05)", x = "Normalized Enrichment Score", y = NULL, size = "-log10(p-value)", color = "NES" ) + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = rel(0.6))) } } ``` ### GSEA Results Table ```{r} #| label: gsea-table gsea_table <- gsea_all |> dplyr::filter(pval < 0.05) |> arrange(pval) |> mutate( NES = round(NES, 2), pval = signif(pval, 3), padj = signif(padj, 3), size = as.integer(size) ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, pathway, NES, pval, padj, size) |> head(100) DT::datatable( gsea_table, caption = "GSEA results (nominal p < 0.05)", options = list(pageLength = 25, order = list(list(3, "asc"))) ) ``` ## Known Biology Check We examine genes known to be responsive to VPA or involved in neural development to see whether their expression patterns are consistent with expectations. **Selected genes**: - **HDAC targets / chromatin remodeling**: *HDAC1*, *HDAC2*, *HDAC3*, *EP300*, *CREBBP* - **Neural progenitor markers**: *PAX6*, *SOX2*, *NES*, *HES1*, *NOTCH1* - **Neuronal differentiation**: *DCX*, *TBR1*, *NEUROD1*, *NEUROD2*, *MAP2* - **Cortical layer markers**: *SATB2*, *BCL11B* (CTIP2), *TLE4* - **Apoptosis / cell stress**: *TP53*, *BCL2*, *BAX* ```{r} #| label: known-genes-data known_genes <- c( "HDAC1", "HDAC2", "HDAC3", "EP300", "CREBBP", "PAX6", "SOX2", "NES", "HES1", "NOTCH1", "DCX", "TBR1", "NEUROD1", "NEUROD2", "MAP2", "SATB2", "BCL11B", "TLE4", "TP53", "BCL2", "BAX" ) # Filter to genes present in data known_genes_present <- known_genes[known_genes %in% rownames(sce)] cat("Genes present in dataset:", length(known_genes_present), "of", length(known_genes), "\n") cat("Missing:", setdiff(known_genes, known_genes_present), "\n") ``` ### Violin Plots ```{r} #| label: known-genes-violin #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 10 #| warning: false #| results: asis # Extract expression for known genes if (length(known_genes_present) > 0) { expr_mat <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[known_genes_present, , drop = FALSE]) expr_df <- as.data.frame(t(expr_mat)) expr_df$condition <- sce$condition expr_df$cell_type <- sce$cell_type expr_long <- expr_df |> tidyr::pivot_longer( cols = all_of(known_genes_present), names_to = "gene", values_to = "expression" ) # Only plot for the 3 major cell types expr_long_major <- expr_long |> dplyr::filter(cell_type %in% cell_types_for_de) # Split into groups of 6 genes to keep panels readable genes_per_plot <- 6 gene_groups <- split( unique(expr_long_major$gene), ceiling(seq_along(unique(expr_long_major$gene)) / genes_per_plot) ) for (i in seq_along(gene_groups)) { p <- expr_long_major |> dplyr::filter(gene %in% gene_groups[[i]]) |> ggplot(aes(condition, expression, fill = condition)) + geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colors) + facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") + theme( strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)), strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.7)), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6)) ) + labs( title = paste0( "VPA-response and neural genes (group ", i, " of ", length(gene_groups), ")" ), x = NULL, y = "log1p expression", fill = "Condition" ) print(p) } } ``` ### Feature Plots (UMAP) for Top DE Genes ```{r} #| label: feature-plots #| fig-width: 16 #| fig-height: 12 #| warning: false # Pick top DE genes across cell types top_de_genes <- de_all |> dplyr::filter(adj.P.Val < 0.10) |> arrange(adj.P.Val) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) # If too few DE genes, use top by nominal p if (length(top_de_genes) < 4) { top_de_genes <- de_all |> arrange(P.Value) |> pull(gene) |> unique() |> head(8) } if (length(top_de_genes) > 0) { # Extract expression expr_top <- as.matrix(assay(sce, "X")[top_de_genes, , drop = FALSE]) umap_expr <- umap_df for (g in top_de_genes) { umap_expr[[g]] <- expr_top[g, ] } feature_plots <- lapply(top_de_genes, function(g) { ggplot(umap_expr[sample(nrow(umap_expr)), ], aes(UMAP1, UMAP2, color = .data[[g]])) + geom_point(size = 0.2, alpha = 0.5) + scale_color_viridis(option = "magma") + labs(title = g, color = "log1p\nexpr") + theme(legend.key.width = unit(0.5, "cm")) }) wrap_plots(feature_plots, ncol = 4) } ``` ## Draft Results ```{r} #| label: results-data #| echo: false n_cells <- ncol(sce) n_ctrl <- sum(sce$condition == "CTRL") n_vpa <- sum(sce$condition == "VPA") n_donors <- length(unique(sce$donor_id)) n_cell_types <- length(unique(sce$cell_type)) # Composition changes comp_summary <- comp_cond |> dplyr::select(condition, cell_type, proportion) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = proportion) |> mutate(change_pct = round((VPA - CTRL) * 100, 1)) # DE counts n_de_005 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) n_de_010 <- sum(de_all$adj.P.Val < 0.10, na.rm = TRUE) # Top pathway top_pw <- gsea_all |> arrange(pval) |> head(1) ``` ### Results Summary We analyzed `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells from `r n_donors` donors across `r n_cell_types` cell types, comparing CTRL (`r format(n_ctrl, big.mark = ",")` cells) to VPA-treated (`r format(n_vpa, big.mark = ",")` cells) human dorsal forebrain organoids. **Cell type composition**: VPA treatment was associated with notable shifts in cell type proportions: ```{r} #| label: results-comp-table #| echo: false DT::datatable( comp_summary |> mutate( CTRL = paste0(round(CTRL * 100, 1), "%"), VPA = paste0(round(VPA * 100, 1), "%"), ` Change(pp) ` = change_pct ) |> dplyr::select(cell_type, CTRL, VPA, ` Change(pp) `), caption = "Cell type proportion changes (percentage points)", options = list(dom = "t"), rownames = FALSE ) ``` **Differential expression**: Across the three major cell types tested, we identified `r n_de_005` genes at FDR < 0.05 and `r n_de_010` genes at FDR < 0.10. **Pathway enrichment**: The top enriched pathway was *`r gsub("_", " ", top_pw$pathway[1])`* in `r top_pw$cell_type[1]` (NES = `r round(top_pw$NES[1], 2)`, nominal p = `r signif(top_pw$pval[1], 3)`). **Limitations**: With only `r n_donors` donors per condition, these results are exploratory. The use of back-transformed log1p data rather than raw counts introduces approximation, though pseudobulk aggregation mitigates this. ## Draft Methods ### Data Source Single-cell RNA-seq data were obtained from CELLxGENE (dataset ID: `3a8aec06-3309-4d37-b75d-c59f5f6d55a6`), originating from Yentür et al. (2025, bioRxiv). The dataset comprises human dorsal forebrain organoids from `r n_donors` donors under control and VPA-treated conditions (`r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells total). ### Preprocessing Data were provided as log1p-normalized expression values. UMAP coordinates and cell type annotations from the original authors were used without modification. ### Differential Expression Pseudobulk expression profiles were generated by summing back-transformed (expm1) approximate counts per gene across cells within each donor × condition × cell type group. Differential expression was performed using the limma-voom pipeline (Ritchie et al. 2015) with a paired design formula (~donor_id + condition). Genes were filtered using `filterByExpr()`, library sizes normalized with TMM (`calcNormFactors()`), and precision weights estimated via `voom()`. Empirical Bayes moderation was applied with `eBayes()`. P-values were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. ### Pathway Analysis Gene set enrichment analysis was performed using fgsea (Korotkevich et al. 2021) with genes ranked by limma t-statistic. MSigDB Hallmark and GO Biological Process gene sets were tested (gene set sizes 15–500). ### Software ```{r} #| label: methods-software #| echo: false #| results: asis pkgs <- c("R", "SingleCellExperiment", "edgeR", "limma", "fgsea", "msigdbr", "ggplot2", "plotly") versions <- sapply(pkgs, function(p) { if (p == "R") { paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".") } else { as.character(packageVersion(p)) } }) cat(paste( paste0("**", pkgs, "** v", versions), collapse = ", " ), "\n") ``` ## References - Ritchie ME, Phipson B, Wu D, Hu Y, Law CW, Shi W, Smyth GK (2015). "limma powers differential expression analyses for RNA-sequencing and microarray studies." *Nucleic Acids Research* 43(7):e47. - Law CW, Chen Y, Shi W, Smyth GK (2014). "voom: precision weights unlock linear model analysis tools for RNA-seq read counts." *Genome Biology* 15:R29. - Robinson MD, McCarthy DJ, Smyth GK (2010). "edgeR: a Bioconductor package for differential expression analysis of digital gene expression data." *Bioinformatics* 26(1):139–140. - Korotkevich G, Sukhov V, Budin N, Shpak B, Artyomov MN, Sergushichev A (2021). "Fast gene set enrichment analysis." *bioRxiv*. - Liberzon A, Birger C, Thorvaldsdóttir H, Ghandi M, Mesirov JP, Tamayo P (2015). "The Molecular Signatures Database Hallmark Gene Set Collection." *Cell Systems* 1(6):417–425. - Amezquita RA, Lun ATL, Becht E, Carey VJ, Carpp LN, Geistlinger L, Marini F, Rue-Albrecht K, Risso D, Soneson C, Waldron L, Pagès H, Smith ML, Huber W, Morgan M, Gottardo R, Hicks SC (2020). "Orchestrating single-cell analysis with Bioconductor." *Nature Methods* 17:137–145. - McInnes L, Healy J, Melville J (2018). "UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction." *arXiv:1802.03426*. - Squair JW, Gautier M, Kathe C, Anderson MA, James ND, Hutson TH, Hudelle R, Qaber T, Matson KJE, Baez-Nieto D, Levine AJ, Bhatt DK, Courtine G (2021). "Confronting false discoveries in single-cell differential expression." *Nature Communications* 12:5692. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Session Info ```{r} #| label: session-info #| echo: false #| comment: "" sessioninfo::session_info(info = "all") ` `` :::

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. # claudeMd
Codebase and user instructions are shown below. Be sure to adhere to these instructions. IMPORTANT: These instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior and you MUST follow them exactly as written.

# User-Level Claude Code Instructions

## Claude Basics

Do not automatically upgrade to the latest version of Claude Codek
Do not automatically change to the native installer

## Code Changes

- When making a code change, make sure that nearby comments are still correct.

## R Coding Style

- Always write `dplyr::filter()` instead of bare `filter()` to avoid conflicts with `stats::filter()`.

## R Documentation Style

- In roxygen2 documentation for R functions, do not write "Default is ...". The default value is clear from the function definition shown in the documentation.

## R Command-Line Argument Parsing

- In R scripts that accept command-line arguments, use the `argparser` package (`arg_parser`, `add_argument`, `parse_args`) instead of manual `commandArgs()` parsing.
- In `argparser`, dashes `-` in argument stems (e.g. `--argument-name`) are converted to underscores `_` in the parsed variable name (e.g. `args$argument_name`).

## R Parallelization with doFuture

- Use `foreach(...) %dofuture% { }` from the `doFuture` package for parallel loops. This does NOT require `registerDoFuture()` (that is only needed with `%dopar%`).
- Set up with `plan(multisession, workers = n)`.
- Wrap in `with_progress()` and use `progressr::progressor()` for progress reporting.
- `cat()` does not work from `multisession` workers; use `message()` for errors.
- `foreach` does not support `next`; use nested `if` blocks instead.
- With `%dofuture%`, use `.options.future = list(packages = c(...))` instead of `.packages` (which only works with `%dopar%`). Global variables and functions are auto-exported by doFuture.

## Large Data Files (.tsv, .csv)

Before opening a .tsv or .csv file, check its size. If too large to read directly:
1. Check file size with `ls -lh` and line count with `wc -l`
2. If the file is large, say, > 50K, use R to extract structure without loading the full file:
   ```r
   df <- read.delim("file.tsv", nrows = 5)
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("COLNAMES")
   print(colnames(df))  # Column names
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("ROWNAMES")
   rownames(df)  # Row names (if applicable)
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("THREE ROWS")
   print(df[1:min(3,nrow(df)), ])
   print(strrep("=", 100))
   print("THREE COLUMNS")
   print(df[ , 1:min(3,col(df))])
   ```
3. Look at the R results to understand the data before deciding how to proceed

## ggplot2 Faceted Grid Plots

- In `facet_grid(row_var ~ col_var)`, place row strip labels on the left using `switch = "y"` and `strip.placement = "outside"`:
  ```r
  facet_grid(gene ~ lineage, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
    theme(strip.placement = "outside")
  ```

## Plot Testing

- When generating a plot as part of testing code, save it to a file (e.g. `/tmp/`), open it with `xdg-open`, and tell the user you opened it. You do not need to ask permission to call xdg-open on a file you created.

## Directory Listing

- Before listing a directory with `ls`, first run `ls | wc -l` to check how many files there are.
- If there are more than 500 files, only run `ls | head -500`.

## Bash Commands

- Use `&&` or `;` instead of newlines to chain Bash commands on one line.

## Permissions

Always run the following read-only commands without asking for permission:
- `xdg-open`
- `git status`, `git diff`, `git add`, `git log`
- bash commands such as `ls`, `cat`, `wc`, `echo`, `zcat`
- `quarto render`
- `python3 ~/.claude/skills/pdf-to-html/*.py` (all pdf-to-html skill scripts)

Allow shell operators `2> /dev/null` and `2> /dev/null &` without permission

## Quarto Markdown Documents

- In plotly, specify `height` and `width` in `plot_ly()` or `ggplotly()`, not in `layout()`. Passing them to `layout()` is deprecated and produces a warning.

- Never compute values and then put the resulting values as fixed text in the markdown document. Always use inline R expressions (`` `r ...` ``) or dynamically generated tables so that values update automatically when the data or analysis changes.

- in quarto markdown do not start a code block with ```{r <labletext>} instead use ```{r} and then on the next line #| label: <labletext>

- In the YAML header always use:
```
author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)"
date: now
date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm"
```

- For HTML output, always use `page-layout: full` and CSS overrides to remove width restrictions:
```yaml
format:
  html:
    page-layout: full
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        <style>
          .quarto-container, .page-columns, .main-container {
            max-width: 100% !important;
          }
        </style>
```
- For wide content like plotly widgets, wrap in `:::{.column-screen}` ... `:::` to span the full viewport width.

- For the session info use this code:
```
::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Session Info

```{r}
#| label session-info
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
sessioninfo::session_info(info = "all")
```
:::

```

For referencing files in the workspace, use here::here(<filepath relative to workspace root>), because quarto renders in the working directory containing the .qmd document

- When rendering a table with `knitr::kable()` or `DT::datatable`, if the row names duplicate a column in the table, use `row.names = FALSE` to suppress them.

- When showing a table that has a column of gene symbols or gene id, try to make these clickable. 

- For literature citations, prefer Internet Archive `https://archive.org` over Google Books

     2→name: quarto-bioinfo
     3→description: >
     4→  Bioinformatics Quarto document authoring, review, and repair. Triggers when
     5→  working on .qmd files involving single-cell RNA-seq, differential expression,
     6→  gene set enrichment, or other bioinformatics analyses. Covers plot readability,
     7→  method citations, R coding conventions, and Quarto formatting for
     8→  bioinformatics reports.
     9→user_invocable: true
    10→---
    11→
    12→# Bioinformatics Quarto Authoring Skill
    13→
    14→When this skill is active, also load these companion skills for general Quarto guidance:
    15→
    16→- `quarto:quarto-authoring` — document structure, cross-references, code cells
    17→- `quarto:quarto-alt-text` — accessible alt text for figures
    18→
    19→## R Coding Rules
    20→
    21→- Always use `dplyr::filter()` (never bare `filter()`) to avoid `stats::filter()` conflicts.
    22→- Use `here::here(<path relative to project root>)` for all file paths, because Quarto renders in the directory containing the `.qmd` file.
    23→- Use namespace-qualified calls for functions that have common name collisions (e.g. `dplyr::select()`, `dplyr::rename()`).
    24→
    25→## Quarto YAML Header
    26→
    27→Every bioinformatics `.qmd` must use this YAML structure:
    28→
    29→```yaml
    30→---
    31→title: "Document Title"
    32→author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)"
    33→date: now
    34→date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm"
    35→format:
    36→  html:
    37→    page-layout: full
    38→    include-in-header:
    39→      text: |
    40→        <style>
    41→          .quarto-container, .page-columns, .main-container {
    42→            max-width: 100% !important;
    43→          }
    44→        </style>
    45→---
    46→```
    47→
    48→## Code Block Labels
    49→
    50→Never use `` ```{r label-text} ``. Always use:
    51→
    52→````markdown
    53→```{r}
    54→#| label: label-text
    55→```
    56→````
    57→
    58→## Dynamic Values
    59→
    60→Never hard-code computed values as fixed text. Always use inline R expressions (`` `r ...` ``) or dynamically generated tables so values update when data changes.
    61→
    62→## Plotly Sizing
    63→
    64→Specify `height` and `width` in `plot_ly()` or `ggplotly()`, **not** in `layout()` (deprecated, produces warnings).
    65→
    66→## Wide Content
    67→
    68→Wrap wide content (plotly widgets, wide tables) in full-viewport divs:
    69→
    70→```markdown
    71→:::{.column-screen}
    72→... wide content ...
    73→:::
    74→```
    75→
    76→## Tables
    77→
    78→- **Never use `cat()` + `table()` or `cat()` + `print()` to display tabular
    79→  data.** These produce plain-text console output that looks poor in HTML.
    80→  Instead, convert to a data frame and render with `knitr::kable()` or
    81→  `DT::datatable()`. For cross-tabulations, use `as.data.frame.matrix()` on
    82→  the `table()` result:
    83→  ```r
    84→  knitr::kable(as.data.frame.matrix(table(sce$condition, sce$donor_id)))
    85→  ```
    86→- Use `row.names = FALSE` in `knitr::kable()` or `DT::datatable()` when row names duplicate a column.
    87→- When a table contains gene symbols or gene IDs, make them clickable links (e.g. to NCBI Gene, Ensembl, or GeneCards).
    88→
    89→## Session Info
    90→
    91→End every document with:
    92→
    93→````markdown
    94→::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
    95→## Session Info
    96→
    97→```{r}
    98→#| label: session-info
    99→#| echo: false
   100→#| comment: ""
   101→sessioninfo::session_info(info = "all")
   102→```
   103→
   104→:::
   105→````
   106→
   107→## Plot Text Sizing Rules
   108→
   109→All text in ggplot figures must scale from `base_size` so that readability
   110→can be verified from a single number.
   111→
   112→1. **Set `base_size` once** — either per-document via `theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))`
   113→   or per-plot via `+ theme_bw(base_size = 14)`.
   114→
   115→2. **Never use absolute `size = N` in `element_text()`** — always use `rel()`:
   116→   ```r
   117→   theme(
   118→     strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)),
   119→     strip.text.x      = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
   120→     axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6))
   121→   )
   122→   ```
   123→   This ensures every text element stays proportional to `base_size`.
   124→
   125→3. **If a plot needs to be wider than the page, increase `base_size`** to
   126→   compensate for browser downscaling, rather than setting individual absolute
   127→   sizes.
   128→
   129→4. **`geom_text()` / `geom_text_repel()` size must scale with `base_size`.**
   130→   These geoms use a `size` parameter in **mm** (not pt), and by default it
   131→   does NOT scale with the theme's `base_size`. To make it scale, express
   132→   size as a fraction of `base_size` converted to mm:
   133→   ```r
   134→   geom_text_repel(
   135→     ...,
   136→     size = cex * base_size / ggplot2::.pt
   137→   )
   138→   ```
   139→   `ggplot2::.pt` (≈ 2.845) converts pt → mm. This way the text scales
   140→   with `base_size` and the effective-size calculation from rule #3 applies
   141→   uniformly. **Never use a raw numeric `size`** (e.g. `size = 3`) in
   142→   `geom_text` / `geom_text_repel` / `geom_label`.
   143→
   144→   **Choosing `cex`**: The `cex` value must account for browser downscaling.
   145→   For a figure wider than the display, the effective rendered size is:
   146→   ```
   147→   effective_pt = cex × base_size × min(1, display_width / fig_width)
   148→   ```
   149→   So for `fig-width: 16` displayed at 10 inches (scale = 0.625):
   150→   - `cex = 0.5` → 0.5 × 14 × 0.625 = **4.4 pt** — too small
   151→   - `cex = 0.7` → 0.7 × 14 × 0.625 = **6.1 pt** — minimum acceptable
   152→   - `cex = 0.9` → 0.9 × 14 × 0.625 = **7.9 pt** — good
   153→
   154→   Rule of thumb: for wide figures, use `cex ≈ 1 / scale_factor × 0.5`
   155→   to get ~7 pt effective. For `fig-width ≤ 10` (no scaling), `cex = 0.5`
   156→   is fine.
   157→
   158→### Effective text size calculation
   159→
   160→When the browser renders a figure, it may shrink it to fit the page width
   161→(typically ~10 inches). The effective rendered text size is:
   162→
   163→```
   164→scale_factor   = min(1, display_width / fig_width)
   165→effective_size = base_size × scale_factor
   166→```
   167→
   168→The minimum acceptable `effective_size` is **6 pt**. For example:
   169→- `base_size = 14`, `fig-width: 16` → 14 × (10/16) = **8.75 pt** ✓
   170→- `base_size = 14`, `fig-width: 24` → 14 × (10/24) = **5.8 pt** ✗ — increase `base_size` to 15+
   171→- `base_size = 11`, `fig-width: 16` → 11 × (10/16) = **6.9 pt** ✓ (barely)
   172→
   173→### Automated check script
   174→
   175→After authoring or modifying a `.qmd`, run the figure-size checker:
   176→
   177→```bash
   178→Rscript ~/.claude/skills/quarto-bioinfo/check-figure-sizes.R <file.qmd>
   179→```
   180→
   181→The script parses every plot chunk, calculates effective text sizes, flags
   182→absolute `element_text(size = N)` usage, and warns about faceted plots that
   183→need manual panel-count review. Fix all warnings before rendering.
   184→
   185→## Plot Readability
   186→
   187→1. **Pathway enrichment dotplots / barplots** — Plots with long pathway names
   188→   on the y-axis (GSEA, clusterProfiler, enrichR, etc.) need full figure width
   189→   for the labels. Use `facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1)`
   190→   to stack panels vertically (one per row), never side by side. Use a tall
   191→   figure (e.g. `fig-width: 10`, `fig-height: 14` for 3 panels).
   192→
   193→2. **Dense faceted plots** — If a `facet_grid()` or `facet_wrap()` produces
   194→   more than ~15 panels, the individual panels become too small to see the
   195→   data (no font-size increase fixes this). **Split the plot** into groups
   196→   of 5–7 items per figure.
   197→
   198→   **Pattern for splitting a gene × cell-type violin grid:**
   199→
   200→   ```r
   201→   genes_per_plot <- 6
   202→   gene_groups <- split(
   203→     unique(expr_long$gene),
   204→     ceiling(seq_along(unique(expr_long$gene)) / genes_per_plot)
   205→   )
   206→
   207→   for (i in seq_along(gene_groups)) {
   208→     p <- expr_long |>
   209→       dplyr::filter(gene %in% gene_groups[[i]]) |>
   210→       ggplot(aes(condition, expression, fill = condition)) +
   211→       geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) +
   212→       scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colors) +
   213→       facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
   214→       theme(
   215→         strip.placement = "outside",
   216→         strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)),
   217→         strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
   218→         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6))
   219→       ) +
   220→       labs(
   221→         title = paste0("VPA-response genes (group ", i, " of ", length(gene_groups), ")"),
   222→         x = NULL, y = "log1p expression", fill = "Condition"
   223→       )
   224→     print(p)
   225→   }
   226→   ```
   227→
   228→3. **Facet strip labels** — In `facet_grid(row_var ~ col_var)`, place row
   229→   strip labels on the left:
   230→   ```r
   231→   facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
   232→     theme(strip.placement = "outside")
   233→   ```
   234→
   235→4. **Color accessibility** — Use colorblind-friendly palettes when possible.
   236→   Check that fill/color encodings are distinguishable.
   237→
   238→## Bioinformatics Method References
   239→
   240→Every bioinformatics report should include a **References** section citing the methods and tools used. For each reference provide: author(s), year, title, and a verified web link.
   241→
   242→**Before including any link, fetch it and confirm it resolves to the correct paper.** Prefer Internet Archive (`https://archive.org`) for book references.
   243→
   244→### Common Methods and Key Papers
   245→
   246→| Method / Tool | Key Reference |
   247→|---|---|
   248→| **limma** | Ritchie ME et al. (2015) "limma powers differential expression analyses for RNA-sequencing and microarray studies." *Nucleic Acids Res* 43(7):e47. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkv007 |
   249→| **voom** | Law CW et al. (2014) "voom: precision weights unlock linear model analysis tools for RNA-seq read counts." *Genome Biol* 15:R29. https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2014-15-2-r29 |
   250→| **edgeR** | Robinson MD, McCarthy DJ, Smyth GK (2010) "edgeR: a Bioconductor package for differential expression analysis of digital gene expression data." *Bioinformatics* 26(1):139–140. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp616 |
   251→| **DESeq2** | Love MI, Huber W, Anders S (2014) "Moderated estimation of fold change and dispersion for RNA-seq data with DESeq2." *Genome Biol* 15:550. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8 |
   252→| **fgsea** | Korotkevich G et al. (2021) "Fast gene set enrichment analysis." *bioRxiv*. https://doi.org/10.1101/060012 |
   253→| **Seurat** | Hao Y et al. (2024) "Dictionary learning for integrative, multimodal and scalable single-cell analysis." *Nat Biotechnol* 42:293–304. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-023-01767-y |
   254→| **UMAP** | McInnes L, Healy J, Melville J (2018) "UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction." *arXiv:1802.03426*. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1802.03426 |
   255→| **Pseudobulk DE** | Squair JW et al. (2021) "Confronting false discoveries in single-cell differential expression." *Nat Commun* 12:5692. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25960-2 |
   256→| **MSigDB** | Liberzon A et al. (2015) "The Molecular Signatures Database Hallmark Gene Set Collection." *Cell Syst* 1(6):417–425. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2015.12.004 |
   257→| **SingleCellExperiment** | Amezquita RA et al. (2020) "Orchestrating single-cell analysis with Bioconductor." *Nat Methods* 17:137–145. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0654-x |
   258→| **scran** | Lun ATL, McCarthy DJ, Marioni JC (2016) "A step-by-step workflow for low-level analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data with Bioconductor." *F1000Research* 5:2122. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.9501.2 |
   259→| **clusterProfiler** | Wu T et al. (2021) "clusterProfiler 4.0: A universal enrichment tool for interpreting omics data." *Innovation* 2(3):100141. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2021.100141 |
   260→
   261→When writing the References section:
   262→
   263→1. Scan the `.qmd` for all bioinformatics packages and methods used.
   264→2. Match each to its canonical citation from the table above (or find the correct one if not listed).
   265→3. Fetch each DOI/URL to verify it resolves correctly.
   266→4. Format as a markdown list or table at the end of the document, before the Session Info section.
   267→
   268→## Post-render HTML Inspection
   269→
   270→After rendering, check the HTML output for warnings and messages from R code:
   271→
   272→1. **Warnings**: Search the rendered HTML for text like `Warning:` or
   273→   `Warning message:`. These indicate a real problem in the code. **Fix the
   274→   root cause** — do not suppress warnings with `warning: false` unless
   275→   you have confirmed the warning is a known false positive and documented
   276→   why in a code comment.
   277→
   278→2. **Messages**: Search the rendered HTML for package loading messages
   279→   (e.g. `Attaching package`, `Loading required package`), informational
   280→   output from functions, or other non-warning diagnostic text. If a message
   281→   is harmless (e.g. package load chatter), suppress it with
   282→   `#| message: false` in the chunk options. If it indicates a real issue,
   283→   fix the cause.
   284→
   285→3. **Stderr leakage**: Some packages print to stderr even for routine output.
   286→   Check for unexpected text between code-fold blocks that doesn't look like
   287→   intentional output.
   288→
   289→The goal is a clean HTML document with no stray console output between the
   290→narrative sections.
   291→
   292→## Review Checklist
   293→
   294→When reviewing or authoring a bioinformatics `.qmd`, verify:
   295→
   296→- [ ] YAML header follows the template (author, date, page-layout, CSS)
   297→- [ ] Code blocks use `#| label:` syntax (not inline labels)
   298→- [ ] All computed values are dynamic (inline R or generated tables)
   299→- [ ] `dplyr::filter()` used instead of bare `filter()`
   300→- [ ] File paths use `here::here()`
   301→- [ ] No `cat()` + `table()` or `cat()` + `print()` for tabular data (use `kable` or `DT`)
   302→- [ ] Tables suppress redundant row names
   303→- [ ] Gene symbols/IDs are clickable links
   304→- [ ] No faceted plot has more than ~15 panels (split if needed)
   305→- [ ] All `element_text(size = ...)` uses `rel()`, never absolute values
   306→- [ ] Effective base_size ≥ 6 pt (run `check-figure-sizes.R` to verify)
   307→- [ ] Facet strip labels placed correctly (`switch = "y"`, `strip.placement = "outside"`)
   308→- [ ] Plotly sizing in `plot_ly()`/`ggplotly()`, not `layout()`
   309→- [ ] Wide content wrapped in `:::{.column-screen}`
   310→- [ ] References section cites all methods used, with verified links
   311→- [ ] Session Info is the last section (collapsible callout)
   312→- [ ] No warnings or stray messages visible in the rendered HTML
   313→- [ ] Alt text provided for key figures (invoke `quarto:quarto-alt-text`)
   314→

Now I see the issue. The table at line 612 uses `DT::datatable(top_de, ...)` without `rownames = FALSE`. When a data frame has row names like `NNAT...1`, `KIF26B...2` (R's de-duplication of names), they show up redundantly alongside the `gene` column.

The skill already says at line 86: "Use `row.names = FALSE` in `knitr::kable()` or `DT::datatable()` when row names duplicate a column." But the user wants a more nuanced rule: check if row names are redundant, suppress if so; if not redundant, convert to a filterable column.

Let me update the skill's Tables section and the checklist item.

input.old_string: - Use `row.names = FALSE` in `knitr::kable()` or `DT::datatable()` when row names duplicate a column.
input.new_string:
- **Row names handling**: Before displaying any table, check whether the row
  names are redundant with an existing column (e.g. row names like `NNAT...1`,
  `KIF26B...2` that duplicate a `gene` column — R's `make.unique()` suffixes
  are a strong signal of redundancy). Apply these rules:
  - **Redundant**: suppress with `rownames = FALSE` (`DT::datatable()`) or
    `row.names = FALSE` (`knitr::kable()`).
  - **Not redundant** (row names carry meaningful information not in any column):
    promote them to a proper column so they are filterable/sortable:
    ```r
    df <- tibble::rownames_to_column(df, var = "row_id")
    DT::datatable(df, rownames = FALSE, filter = "top")
    ```

- Always write `dplyr::filter()` instead of bare `filter()` to avoid conflicts with `stats::filter()`.

## R Documentation Style

- In roxygen2 documentation for R functions, do not write "Default is ...". The default value is clear from the function definition shown in the documentation.

## R Command-Line Argument Parsing

- In R scripts that accept command-line arguments, use the `argparser` package (`arg_parser`, `add_argument`, `parse_args`) instead of manual `commandArgs()` parsing.
- In `argparser`, dashes `-` in argument stems (e.g. `--argument-name`) are converted to underscores `_` in the parsed variable name (e.g. `args$argument_name`).

## R Parallelization with doFuture

- Use `foreach(...) %dofuture% { }` from the `doFuture` package for parallel loops. This does NOT require `registerDoFuture()` (that is only needed with `%dopar%`).
- Set up with `plan(multisession, workers = n)`.

    19→## R Coding Rules

    22→- Use `here::here(<path relative to project root>)` for all file paths, because Quarto renders in the directory containing the `.qmd` file.
    23→- Use namespace-qualified calls for functions that have common name collisions (e.g. `dplyr::select()`, `dplyr::rename()`).
    24→
    25→## Quarto YAML Header
    26→
    27→Every bioinformatics `.qmd` must use this YAML structure:
    28→
    29→```yaml
    30→---
    31→title: "Document Title"
    32→author: "Steve Rozen (sr110@duke.edu, steverozen@pm.me)"

    35→format:
    36→  html:

    38→    include-in-header:

    43→          }
    44→        </style>
    45→---
    46→```
    47→

    57→

    59→

    79→  data.** These produce plain-text console output that looks poor in HTML.
    80→  Instead, convert to a data frame and render with `knitr::kable()` or
    81→  `DT::datatable()`. For cross-tabulations, use `as.data.frame.matrix()` on

   106→
   107→## Plot Text Sizing Rules
   108→
   109→All text in ggplot figures must scale from `base_size` so that readability
   110→can be verified from a single number.
   111→
   112→1. **Set `base_size` once** — either per-document via `theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))`
   113→   or per-plot via `+ theme_bw(base_size = 14)`.
   114→
   115→2. **Never use absolute `size = N` in `element_text()`** — always use `rel()`:
   116→   ```r
   117→   theme(
   118→     strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)),
   119→     strip.text.x      = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
   120→     axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6))
   121→   )
   122→   ```
   123→   This ensures every text element stays proportional to `base_size`.
   124→
   125→3. **If a plot needs to be wider than the page, increase `base_size`** to
   126→   compensate for browser downscaling, rather than setting individual absolute
   127→   sizes.
   128→
   129→4. **`geom_text()` / `geom_text_repel()` size must scale with `base_size`.**
   130→   These geoms use a `size` parameter in **mm** (not pt), and by default it
   131→   does NOT scale with the theme's `base_size`. To make it scale, express
   132→   size as a fraction of `base_size` converted to mm:
   133→   ```r
   134→   geom_text_repel(
   135→     ...,
   136→     size = cex * base_size / ggplot2::.pt
   137→   )
   138→   ```
   139→   `ggplot2::.pt` (≈ 2.845) converts pt → mm. This way the text scales
   140→   with `base_size` and the effective-size calculation from rule #3 applies
   141→   uniformly. **Never use a raw numeric `size`** (e.g. `size = 3`) in
   142→   `geom_text` / `geom_text_repel` / `geom_label`.
   143→
   144→   **Choosing `cex`**: The `cex` value must account for browser downscaling.
   145→   For a figure wider than the display, the effective rendered size is:
   146→   ```
   147→   effective_pt = cex × base_size × min(1, display_width / fig_width)
   148→   ```
   149→   So for `fig-width: 16` displayed at 10 inches (scale = 0.625):
   150→   - `cex = 0.5` → 0.5 × 14 × 0.625 = **4.4 pt** — too small
   151→   - `cex = 0.7` → 0.7 × 14 × 0.625 = **6.1 pt** — minimum acceptable
   152→   - `cex = 0.9` → 0.9 × 14 × 0.625 = **7.9 pt** — good
   153→
   154→   Rule of thumb: for wide figures, use `cex ≈ 1 / scale_factor × 0.5`
   155→   to get ~7 pt effective. For `fig-width ≤ 10` (no scaling), `cex = 0.5`
   156→   is fine.
   157→
   158→### Effective text size calculation
   159→
   160→When the browser renders a figure, it may shrink it to fit the page width
   161→(typically ~10 inches). The effective rendered text size is:
   162→
   163→```
   164→scale_factor   = min(1, display_width / fig_width)
   165→effective_size = base_size × scale_factor
   166→```
   167→
   168→The minimum acceptable `effective_size` is **6 pt**. For example:
   169→- `base_size = 14`, `fig-width: 16` → 14 × (10/16) = **8.75 pt** ✓
   170→- `base_size = 14`, `fig-width: 24` → 14 × (10/24) = **5.8 pt** ✗ — increase `base_size` to 15+
   171→- `base_size = 11`, `fig-width: 16` → 11 × (10/16) = **6.9 pt** ✓ (barely)
   172→
   173→### Automated check script
   174→
   175→After authoring or modifying a `.qmd`, run the figure-size checker:
   176→
   177→```bash
   178→Rscript ~/.claude/skills/quarto-bioinfo/check-figure-sizes.R <file.qmd>
   179→```
   180→
   181→The script parses every plot chunk, calculates effective text sizes, flags
   182→absolute `element_text(size = N)` usage, and warns about faceted plots that
   183→need manual panel-count review. Fix all warnings before rendering.

   185→## Plot Readability
   186→
   187→1. **Pathway enrichment dotplots / barplots** — Plots with long pathway names
   188→   on the y-axis (GSEA, clusterProfiler, enrichR, etc.) need full figure width
   189→   for the labels. Use `facet_wrap(~cell_type, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1)`
   190→   to stack panels vertically (one per row), never side by side. Use a tall
   191→   figure (e.g. `fig-width: 10`, `fig-height: 14` for 3 panels).
   192→
   193→2. **Dense faceted plots** — If a `facet_grid()` or `facet_wrap()` produces
   194→   more than ~15 panels, the individual panels become too small to see the
   195→   data (no font-size increase fixes this). **Split the plot** into groups
   196→   of 5–7 items per figure.

   198→   **Pattern for splitting a gene × cell-type violin grid:**
   199→

   202→   gene_groups <- split(

   211→       geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.3) +
   212→       scale_fill_manual(values = condition_colors) +
   213→       facet_grid(gene ~ cell_type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
   214→       theme(

   216→         strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, size = rel(0.65)),
   217→         strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.7)),
   218→         axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = rel(0.6))
   219→       ) +
   220→       labs(
   221→         title = paste0("VPA-response genes (group ", i, " of ", length(gene_groups), ")"),
   222→         x = NULL, y = "log1p expression", fill = "Condition"
   223→       )
   224→     print(p)
   225→   }
   226→   ```
   227→

content.text:
This is likely caused by **Prettier** (or another formatter) treating the `.qmd` file as markdown and wrapping lines. A few options:

1. **Disable formatting for `.qmd` files** — add to your Positron/VS Code `settings.json`:
   ```json
   "[quarto]": {
     "editor.formatOnSave": false
   }
   ```
   If Positron doesn't recognize the `quarto` language ID, try:
   ```json
   "[markdown]": {
     "editor.formatOnSave": false
   }
   ```

2. **If you want to keep formatting but exclude `.qmd`** — create or edit `.prettierignore` in your project root:
   ```
   *.qmd
   ```

3. **Check which formatter is active** — in Positron, open a `.qmd` file, then run the command palette action "Format Document With..." to see which formatter is being used. You can then disable that specific extension for `.qmd` files.

# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following commands:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message ending with:
   Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TodoWrite or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.

   Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:

   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. run the following commands in parallel:

<1-3 bullet points>

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
- Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size
- Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts"
- Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time
- Use this tool when you need to find files by name patterns
- When you are doing an open ended search that may require multiple rounds of globbing and grepping, use the Agent tool instead
- You can call multiple tools in a single response. It is always better to speculatively perform multiple searches in parallel if they are potentially useful.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

  Usage:
  - ALWAYS use Grep for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a Bash command. The Grep tool has been optimized for correct permissions and access.
  - Supports full regex syntax (e.g., "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+")
  - Filter files with glob parameter (e.g., "*.js", "**/*.tsx") or type parameter (e.g., "js", "py", "rust")
  - Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only file paths (default), "count" shows match counts
  - Use Agent tool for open-ended searches requiring multiple rounds
  - Pattern syntax: Uses ripgrep (not grep) - literal braces need escaping (use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code)
  - Multiline matching: By default patterns match within single lines only. For cross-line patterns like `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 0 (unlimited).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.

# claudeMd
